Weakly Conditioned Diffusion Model Augmentation for Prostate Segmentation

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (235 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.34230v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep learning models for prostate MRI segmentation often struggle to generalize when trained on limited heterogeneous data, leading to boundary errors and over-segmentation. We present an augmentation framework using mask-conditioned synthetic and diverse T2-weighted MRI volumes to improve boundary precision and reduce over-segmentation. We employ a 2.5D weakly mask-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) via channel concatenation. The diffusion model conditions on stacks of adjacent binary masks from training folds. The model generates T2 volumes consistent with the conditioning anatomy while diversifying tissue appearance. We evaluate the proposed approach on two cohorts of data: (i) the LUND probe cohort (n=432) for strategy selection and training nnU-Net from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix, and (ii) the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) prostate cohort (n=32) evaluated with a 20% synthetic data mix. For the LUND cohort, we found that training an nnU-Net model from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix reduced the mean false-positive voxels per case from 11,102 (baseline) to 10,757. On the MSD cohort, the augmented model with a 20% synthetic mix achieved a mean cross-validated Dice of 0.9094, improving over the baseline (0.8935) by 1.59 percentage points and reducing mean false-positive voxels by 23.1% (4,201 to 3,229). Experimental results on both these cohorts suggest that mask-conditioned DDPM augmentation can reduce over-segmentation errors and improve boundary adherence in data-constrained settings.

#43341. Breaking: The Socratic PAUSE: safeguarding scientific judgement at AI speed

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (243 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The Socratic PAUSE: safeguarding scientific judgement at AI speed

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (243 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34222v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative AI can turn a tentative scientific question into hypotheses, methods, code and interpretations within minutes. Yet generating a contribution does not establish that it deserves scientific reliance: researchers must still examine its evidence, assumptions and implications, and remain accountable for the decision to rely on it. Using Einstein's sketch of scientific discovery as a lens, we argue that AI has accelerated discovery far more than justification. In human-AI research partnerships, confidence can therefore outgrow evidence through three mechanisms: recursive reinforcement, loss of provenance and miscalibrated reliance on AI-generated contributions. Verification debt accumulates when such contributions are carried into later claims or decisions without adequate scrutiny. Accordingly, we propose the Socratic Pause as a deliberate checkpoint at consequential decision gates, where an AI contribution remains provisional while a researcher examines its basis. The PAUSE protocol structures this examination through five steps: Pin down the claim, Ask and challenge, Uncover assumptions and alternatives, Scrutinise the evidence and Exercise judgement. It concludes with a recorded decision to accept, revise, reject or defer the contribution. We show how AI research tools can support this practice without displacing human judgement, and outline a framework for evaluating whether it improves verification, decision-making and independent understanding. The aim is to preserve the freedom to explore with AI while ensuring that those responsible for the work can say what was examined, what remains uncertain and why the next step is justified.

GeoCAM: Self-Supervised Sonar-Optical Representation Learning via Geographic Overlap Supervision

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (188 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34218v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cross-modal self-supervised learning for paired side-scan sonar and underwater optical imagery is a promising direction for benthic habitat understanding, but it remains underexplored because existing methods do not fully exploit the one-to-many correspondences and geographic metadata available in real opti-acoustic surveys. This limits the ability to learn representations that are both semantically meaningful and geometrically consistent from abundant unlabeled marine data. To address this problem, we present GeoCAM, a geography-guided framework that learns a shared embedding space for sonar tiles and their associated optical views without semantic annotations. GeoCAM achieves its goal by combining three components: (i) a Set Attention Aggregator that adaptively summarizes multiple optical observations into a single tile-level representation; (ii) a geometry-weighted InfoNCE objective that converts GPS-derived footprint overlap into soft positive supervision; and (iii) an optional cross-modal masked reconstruction branch that encourages physically grounded cross-modal alignment. Experiments on the BenthiCat SSS-CAM dataset show that GeoCAM can be effectively exploited to learn which sonar and camera samples describe the same seabed patch, improving cross-modal retrieval and alignment over strong contrastive baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/FadiZidiDz/GeoCAM.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the past year, more than 20,000 transitioning servicemembers and veterans have claimed a year of ChatGPT Plus at no cost after being offered free access by OpenAI. That milestone gives us a chance to look at how veterans are using AI to prepare for civilian careers and to figure out what comes next for themselves and their families.

In a recent development, the effort started with veterans who work here at OpenAI, people who use these tools every day and know firsthand how challenging the transition can be. Beyond the free access, OpenAI Academy and our community partners have hosted more than a dozen trainings for nearly 1,000 members of the military community, with seven more⁠(opens in a new window) scheduled before the year ends.

According to recent reports, leaving the military often means stepping into an unfamiliar job market and working out how years of service translate into a civilian role. Many veterans are turning to ChatGPT to organize their job search, rehearse for interviews, and explore paths they hadn’t considered.

Air Force veteran Tilak Bhatnagar⁠(opens in a new window) used his free year to prepare for a dozen interviews, find the right words to describe his military experience to civilian employers, and weigh competing job offers. Along the way, those conversations helped him clarify what he actually wanted from life after active duty.

Recent findings suggest that he ultimately took a role at a tech company. What he valued most was being able to pick up where he left off, returning to the same thread about his background, goals, and constraints. As he put it, “each conversation built on the last.”.

In a recent development, sadarian Bell⁠(opens in a fresh window), also an Air Force veteran, started planning more than a year before he left the service. He used ChatGPT to map out his transition and to turn nearly a decade of military healthcare experience into a civilian résumé.

To prepare for interviews, he practiced out loud using ChatGPT voice mode, working through one question at a time until his answers felt natural. “It has genuinely become my career coach,” Sadarian stated, though he also learned to recognize when he’d had enough help and could trust his own judgment.

For Navy veteran Kelli Ramirez⁠(opens in a upcoming window), the transition was a chance to chase a long-held dream: becoming a published author. She’d already invested in a book-writing course to sharpen her craft, and ChatGPT filled in the gaps. “ChatGPT helped me organize ideas, ask questions about publishing, and work through the Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing process,” she said.

Kelli has since published two books, which she says “reflect my desire to help women approach technology with confidence and, for those who share my Christian faith, with wisdom grounded in that faith.”.

Not everyone arrives confident about using AI tools, which is why OpenAI Academy gives veterans, transitioning servicemembers, and military spouses a place to learn alongside people who understand what they’re going through.

In a recent development, openAI recently wrapped our first six-event Academy series with Veterans Forge⁠(opens in a upcoming window), focused on helping veterans and military families use ChatGPT to work toward their goals. That pilot, together with workshops alongside AI Collective Hampton Roads and NPower, is shaping what we offer veterans next.

At one workshop in Reston, Virginia⁠(opens in a latest window), nearly 100 veterans and active-duty servicemembers⁠(opens in a new window) explored ways to put AI to work. Participant Ryan Kaono-Wedemeyer⁠(opens in a new window) learned to start by writing out a detailed account of his military experience, then asking AI to help shape it into a civilian résumé.

Instructor Erin Marie⁠(opens in a upcoming window) helped participants build custom GPTs to support their transitions, and watched people who walked in skeptical begin finding ways the tools could genuinely help them.

In Louisville, Kentucky, more than 80 Legionnaires⁠(opens in a fresh window) attended three AI training sessions at the American Legion’s national convention. For those who can’t make it to an event, our online veterans collection⁠(opens in a new window) and 100 chats for veterans⁠(opens in a new window) offer examples to try on your own.

We’re continuing this work with partners across the country through the rest of the year:.

Recent findings suggest that november 12: NPower event in St. Louis⁠(opens in a fresh window).

November 14: Nashville event with Veterans Forge and Wounded Warrior Project⁠(opens in a upcoming window).

November 17: 30-minute virtual session⁠(opens in a new window).

November 19: NPower event in Dallas⁠(opens in a new window).

November 21: NPower event in San Antonio⁠(opens in a upcoming window).

Our goal is to help veterans and military families carry the skills they built in service into whatever work they choose next. We’re grateful to ID.me⁠(opens in a new window) for helping servicemembers and veterans access the free-year offer, and to our community partners for making these events possible.

This Veterans Day, OpenAI thanks veterans for their service and for contributing to their communities.

See if you’re eligible for a free year of ChatGPT Plus.⁠(opens in a new window).

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • ⚡ Quick Read (148 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Beyond Logits: Coherent Hallucination Mitigation via Attention Contrastive Decoding

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (148 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.34207v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate impressive multimodal capabilities, yet suffer from hallucination - generating factually inaccurate content. Contrastive Decoding (CD) mitigates this by contrasting amateur and expert branches at the logit level. However, our investigation reveals that such logit-level interventions fundamentally compromise generation coherence, necessitating restrictive penalty constraints unrelated to hallucination suppression. We introduce Attention Contrastive Decoding (ACD), a training-free plug-in that complements logit-level CD by relocating part of the contrastive operations to the attention mechanism. Operating at an earlier stage of the forward pass, ACD performs smooth semantic-preserving interventions through an Adaptive Subtraction Strategy (ASS), which attenuates hallucination-associated attention patterns while amplifying critical visual information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that combining ACD with existing CD methods (e.g., VCD+ACD) produces substantially more coherent outputs with further reduced hallucinations, eliminating restrictive penalties while enabling trustworthy multimodal generation.

Gilbert + Tobin rethinks the business of law with AI

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A conversation with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin.
  • Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.
  • It has been revealed that gilbert + Tobin⁠(opens in a upcoming window) is one of Australia’s leading corporate law firms, with work spanning capital markets, mergers and acquisitions, disputes, and technology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A conversation with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin.

Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.

It has been revealed that gilbert + Tobin⁠(opens in a upcoming window) is one of Australia’s leading corporate law firms, with work spanning capital markets, mergers and acquisitions, disputes, and technology. The firm operates in a profession built on specialist knowledge, careful judgement, and the secure handling of sensitive information.

Gilbert + Tobin began by giving its people room to experiment with AI, then introduced ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Work and Codex to move from individual assistance to defined, multistep agentic workflows, with people responsible for review and approval.

We spoke with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin, about leading adoption from the front, where he’s seeing the value of AI, and his advice for other CEOs.

We have three objectives: to use AI to deliver better services to our clients, make Gilbert + Tobin a great place to work for our people and firmly establish ourselves as a leader in our market.

The real value we’ve seen from AI so far hasn’t been about reducing cost or needing fewer people, but freeing our people to focus on the more human side of their work, meeting with clients, coaching their teams and mentoring the future leaders of our industry.

“It’s been about…freeing them up to then do the more human side of their work.”.

When ChatGPT first became available, we encouraged people to experiment with it and think about where it might create value. We were clear that no client data or confidential information should be entered. That gave people a safe, constrained environment to experiment.

The next step was to provide a secure channel to powerful AI. We introduced ChatGPT Enterprise in a controlled environment and expanded from there. Australian data residency, contractual protections, role-based access and administrative controls gave us the confidence to scale while meeting our requirements and those of our clients.

Governance should enable responsible use. Our message was simple: AI is not cheating. It is another tool people can use to apply their judgement. They still need to define the task, check the output and take responsibility for the final work.

Recent findings suggest that leaders have to use the technology themselves: experiment, push the boundaries and learn what works. When people see that AI matters to you, it sets the tone and encourages others to engage with it.

We did not mandate usage targets. Instead, we made the technology relevant. Our business transformation team demonstrated workflows tailored to different functions, while videos, showcases, challenges and an early AI bounty surfaced ideas from across the firm.

Gilbert + Tobin has always been willing to lean into new technology. What has been most encouraging is the creativity coming from every part of the organisation – not only the technology team.

“Getting started yourself…sets the tone and encourages others.”.

Recent findings suggest that to help manage my workload more effectively, I created a “digital twin” through a custom GPT (now shifting to Plugins) using examples of my writing, feedback I had received, context about the firm and the way I like to work. It started as a tool for me and became more valuable when I shared it with my direct reports.

My team is now able to use it to get “my feedback”, effectively, via ChatGPT. It lets them test their thinking against my context and working style before coming to me. It does not make decisions or speak for me; it helps our conversations start from a stronger place.

I also used ChatGPT Work in a confidential annual review process involving our 120 partners. I asked it to update files with data from a spreadsheet, create PDFs and bundle the finished material. It completed the work in minutes.

In a recent development, with a product as powerful as ChatGPT Work, it’s vital to have the right admin controls behind the scenes, and it now provides detailed, granular data on usage. When I checked the usage dashboard afterwards, the cost for that annual review work was about $62. That was a good trade for the time I saved – and for work that would otherwise have required several other people over multiple days.

According to recent reports, start by using the technology yourself. Experiment with real work, understand its limitations and show your people that learning matters.

Pair that leadership with clear governance and practical enablement. Give teams examples tailored to their roles, create safe ways to test ideas and keep people responsible for the result.

The opportunity is bigger than doing the same work a little more quickly. Used well, AI can raise the quality and volume of what an organisation produces – and give people more time for the complex, strategic work where their expertise and judgement create the greatest value.

MINE: A Training-Free Defense against Indirect Prompt Injection via Mutual Information and Embedding Variance

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (148 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34188v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing defenses against indirect prompt injection in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are inherently reactive: prompt-engineering methods are often overridden by the injected instructions, while supervised detectors must be retrained for each new attack style. We propose a different paradigm: defend by maximizing relevance, not by detecting attacks. Our method, MINE, is training-free and attack-agnostic, and it also serves as a query-conditioned reranker. To evaluate defenses under realistic conditions, we introduce LC-Inj-SQuAD, a long-context benchmark with an average of 4,032 words per context. We evaluate on four datasets spanning short-context QA (Inj-SQuAD, Inj-TriviaQA), long-context QA (LC-Inj-SQuAD), and agent tool-call injection (InjecAgent). Across all four, MINE achieves the best accuracy--security trade-off among training-free defenses. It is also the only defense that stays usable against a fully adaptive attacker, generalizes to agent tool-call injection, and achieves the lowest inference latency on long contexts.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (188 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.34184v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) in real-world systems must handle unpredictable modality missingness caused by sensor failures, privacy masking, and unstable transmission. Existing methods either learn reliability-aware representations or reconstruct missing inputs, often using a single flattened encoder output. This overlooks deep encoders' semantic hierarchy and intra- and inter-modal interactions, causing semantic averaging and ill-posed mappings. We propose Hierarchical Semantic Learning (HSL), a framework that exploits semantic hierarchy for robust MSA with missing modalities. Hierarchical Semantic Decoupling exposes low-, mid-, and high-level feature streams from each modality encoder. Cross-Modal Cross-Level Semantic Reconstruction performs ladder-style recovery, using high-level semantics from observed modalities as global anchors to progressively reconstruct mid-level structures and low-level details of missing modalities. To stabilize cross-level reconstruction, Hierarchical Cascade Error Supervisor applies prototypical contrastive regularization to observed and reconstructed features, enforcing level-specific semantic consistency and limiting error propagation. Finally, Hierarchical Interactive Fusion captures dense interactions across modalities and semantic levels to produce robust predictions under diverse missingness patterns. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, IEMOCAP, and CH-SIMS show that HSL outperforms baselines in most missing-modality settings.

In such settings, multiple agents must anticipate both teammate behavior and opponent actions. We study a hybrid predict-then-optimize approach for assigning controllable agents to objectives in real time. Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.34152v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at static visual understanding and are increasingly applied to spatial planning, where a model interprets a visual layout and outputs an action sequence to reach a goal. Grid games are a common testbed for this ability because their rules are explicit and a solver can verify every move. Yet existing benchmarks mostly report end-to-end success rates, which hide whether a failure stems from visual perception, rule application, or multi-step planning. We introduce GridProbe, a diagnostic benchmark that 1) locates the failing stage between visual perception and planning and 2) verifies the diagnosis by targeted fine-tuning. On Sokoban, GridProbe pairs end-to-end solving with four probes (recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state tracking) and gives every board both as an image and as an equivalent text grid. Evaluating seven MLLMs on Sokoban and a maze game reveals distinct bottlenecks behind similar success rates: proprietary models are limited by multi-step planning, whereas open-source models are limited by rule application or by visual grid indexing, i.e., counting rows and columns. Planning failures also hide perception failures: when planning is easier, the visual cost of the same model grows from 7.6 to 37.7 points. The diagnosis identifies what to train: fine-tuning only the vision module of the perception-limited model on board reading raises its interactive Sokoban success 3.5-fold (5.8% to 20.4%) and transfers zero-shot to the unseen maze game (single-turn success 13.8% to 67.1%), whereas the same data does not help a rule-limited model and training on solver solutions brings no gain. We will release the benchmark and code at https://github.com/suat-llm/GridProbe.

OpenAI pledges $2 million as part of a global effort to better understand AI’s impact on children and support their safety and wellbeing.

Earlier this week at the Paris Peace Forum, OpenAI signed the Charter of Engagement for Safer AI for Children⁠(opens in a fresh window) and committed $2 million to support the scientific research network under the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of AI.

This builds on our call for global standards on youth AI safety, and sustained collaboration among governments, researchers, civil society and industry to translate shared evidence into practical safeguards.

Our contribution supports shared measurement work: developing tools researchers can use to better understand and measure AI’s risks and opportunities for children, helping inform safer products and better policy.

Industry observers note that the charter sets out shared principles for safe, age-appropriate AI, alongside a research programme and safeguards for its independence. Research teams retain control over their conclusions, and findings will be published, including negative or inconclusive results.

According to recent reports, this work will help build the evidence needed to support the benefits of AI for young people while addressing risks to their safety and development. It builds on our support for comprehensive youth AI safety legislation that establishes strong, enforceable protections while preserving access to tools for learning, creativity and opportunity. Such frameworks should include age-appropriate safeguards by default, tools for parents, regular risk assessments and mitigation, and meaningful accountability. We look forward to engaging with European policymakers as the EU Kids Act develops, and with partners around the world to advance stronger protections and opportunities for young people.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.34142v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agentic review systems are increasingly flagging suspected bugs in Linux kernel patches as textual reports. A maintainer who receives such reports needs further inspection to determine whether the report is true. The inspection requires understanding whether the bug can be triggered and, if necessary, manually constructing one. As a consequence, despite the excessive textual explanation, many reports go unanswered. In this paper, we argue that a runnable proof-of-concept (PoC) is the key information in such AI-generated kernel review reports. It is, however, challenging to automatically synthesize a valid and runnable PoC. We present ReproCue, a framework that generates PoCs for AI-generated Linux kernel reviews. ReproCue replays the historical kernel bugs and learns one reproduction finite-state-machine (FSM) per subsystem from successful runs. An FSM records the steps a reproduction goes through, together with the requirements observed at each step. Given a new review, ReproCue follows the FSM of that subsystem, adjusting the PoC and the environment as execution reveals what is missing. In 100 recent AI-generated reviews, ReproCue writes PoCs for 49 of them, compared with 10 for the current agentic reproducer and 9 for the state-of-the-art directed fuzzing. Excitingly, with our generated PoCs, Linux kernel maintainers confirmed 69.4% of them, much higher than 9.3% from Sashiko where only textual explanations are included, making AI reviews more actionable in practice.

Compared with general-purpose video generation, robotics places more stringent requirements on world models. Generated videos must satisfy fine-grained physical constraints on robot motion and object interactions. To address this problem, we introduce WorldPhy, a world model benchmark for accurate, fine-grained evaluation of physical plausibility in robotics. Our benchmark contains 300 tasks, each consisting of an initial-frame image and a task instruction, covering diverse robotics scenes, task categories, viewpoints, and robot configurations. We further collect over 12K high-quality human annotations, and use them to train WorldPhyReward to accurately provide scores and reasons across six fine-grained physical dimensions and an instruction-following dimension. Comparisons with general VLMs and existing reward models show that WorldPhyReward better aligns with human ratings. We system- atically evaluate 13 frontier open and closed-source world models. The results reveal that current world models struggle to consistently maintain fine-grained physical plausibility across different robotics scenarios. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Industry observers note that holiday Extras⁠(opens in a fresh window) helps customers search, book and manage trips. For CEO Matthew Pack, becoming an AI-based travel technology business means changing how the whole organisation works: giving the people who understand customers and operations the ability to improve them directly.

Tech giant-wide ChatGPT Enterprise access established the foundation. Codex extended it into building software, from customer-facing apps to internal systems. Pack builds with Codex himself, using that experience to understand what colleagues need and raise his expectations of what the business can achieve.

Sources indicate that holiday Extras had spent years developing its mobile apps⁠(opens in a fresh window). Major changes to its main app centred on an annual release. With Codex, it challenged itself to rethink the experience and how it was built.

Industry observers note that within two weeks, the team had a fully working rebuild, achieving development progress that previously would have taken over six months. Liam Thompson, VP of AI Innovation and formerly Head of Design, worked with engineers to translate his understanding of customers into software. Small, documented packages created reusable foundations, while engineers focused on architecture, APIs, security and development workflows.

Industry observers note that the rebuilt app offered a more personal experience informed by customers’ bookings, trips and history. Codex enabled iOS and Android features to be developed together, bringing improvements to both platforms without Android following behind.

Higher conversion: open-to-book conversion on the main app increased 32.5% following the rebuild.

Fewer errors: the main app’s error rate fell from 19% to 9%.

More frequent improvements: the main app moved from an annual major release to weekly releases in the first month after the rebuild, each containing multiple new features.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.34126v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In real-world applications like egocentric recording, visual accessibility, and surveillance review, visual evidence for Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) is often only partially captured. A reliable model should match its response to the evidence: answering when sufficient, guessing from visible clues when partial, and abstaining when absent. Yet existing benchmarks enforce a binary answerable-or-unanswerable split, leaving partial evidence unmeasured and obscuring whether failures arise from missing evidence or misjudging sufficiency. We introduce ClueProbe, a diagnostic benchmark to (1) separate perceiving evidence from judging sufficiency, and (2) validate our diagnosis via targeted fine-tuning. ClueProbe comprises 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, alongside controlled perturbations altering wording or visual input. Evaluating 10 open-source and proprietary Video LLMs reveals that failures stem from judgment rather than perception: models perceive the evidence yet lack graded sufficiency awareness, answering or refusing outright while rarely guessing from partial clues. Targeted fine-tuning shows that this reflects missing supervision rather than insufficient capacity: supervising the guess level lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/suat-llm/ClueProbe.

arXiv:2611.34122v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) allows a wireless system to use the same waveform for communication and environment sensing. At mmWave frequency bands, ISAC enables diverse human sensing tasks, such as localization, gesture recognition, and pose estimation, with high precision. However, each task requires training a dedicated model, typically from scratch on a task-specific dataset, with no mechanism to flag unreliable predictions. This hurts the scalability, transferability, and reliability of mmWave ISAC models. In this work, we propose MUSE (Multi-task Uncertainty-aware Self-supervised Encoder), a unified framework for mmWave human sensing. MUSE leverages a self-supervised transformer model with per-dataset tokenization and is trained via masked autoencoding across five datasets. During fine-tuning, MUSE uses evidential classification heads that enable uncertainty quantification. MUSE replaces N separate encoders with a single shared transformer encoder, an N-times backbone parameter reduction, while achieving a 9.7 percentage points improvement in classification performance compared to the task-specific model, showing that learning jointly across tasks improves per-task generalization. Across four classification tasks, MUSE produces reliable uncertainty estimates that enable selective prediction, improving accuracy by abstaining on the least confident 20% of predictions. We further improve the reliability of the model's confidence estimates using temperature scaling and conformal prediction. Finally, MUSE's uncertainty signal remains reliable even under cross-user deployment, assigning higher uncertainty to wrong predictions than to correct ones 78% of the time, and recovering 9.2 percentage points of accuracy through selective prediction, with no additional retraining on the unseen user.

In this work, we study whether a drone agent's action boundary is stable under changes to the target descriptor. We evaluate recent and popular LLMs in a simulated perception-action pipeline over real-world drone imagery, where models can localize requested targets and invoke a simulated lethal tool. In a recent development, arXiv:2611.34106v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Symbolic regression seeks to discover interpretable governing equations for dynamical systems from data. In systems biology, however, accurately reproducing system trajectories does not necessarily imply recovery of the underlying reaction mechanisms. Existing benchmarks evaluate numerical accuracy, expression complexity, or equation-level similarity, but not agreement between recovered reactions and reference mechanisms in biological systems. We introduce SysBio-SR, a benchmark of 198 literature-based biological ODE systems with reaction annotations spanning mass action, Michaelis--Menten, Hill, and complex kinetics. Trajectory fidelity is evaluated across all systems under in-distribution reconstruction and out-of-distribution (OOD) extrapolation, while mechanism recovery is assessed on the subset of 161 systems. We evaluate trajectory fidelity across 11 symbolic-discovery methods and assess mechanism recovery for three reaction-based methods. Joint analysis across systems highlights how severely trajectory-based evaluation overestimates true mechanism recovery. Motivated by these findings, we develop KineSelect, a framework that searches candidate reaction topologies under biologically grounded kinetic laws to select optimal mechanisms that balance trajectory fidelity with structural parsimony. Compared with the strongest baseline, KineSelect improves aggregate OOD extrapolation \(R^2\) by 19.2\% and overall reaction F1 score by 14.3\%.

Under Vietnam's 2025 unified-clearing reform, exact filling falls to 10.4%, H-Soft and capped L1 tie quotas (p = 0.979), and 90% cluster-weighted conformal coverage drops from 89.3% to 74.6%. According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.34101v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Precipitation nowcasting requires accurate short-term predictions under rapidly evolving spatiotemporal dynamics. Generative diffusion models can produce detailed and competitive radar forecasts by modeling conditional distributions. However, most existing approaches rely on separately trained components, such as deterministic branches or latent compression modules. More fundamentally, distribution matching alone fails to explicitly optimize operational forecast skill. We propose AlignPre, a streamlined pixel-space nowcasting framework that bridges this gap via skill-aligned post-training (SAPT). AlignPre employs an end-to-end flow-matching forecaster with a hierarchical spatiotemporal architecture for distribution matching and direct radar-field synthesis, without latent compression. During post-training, SAPT exploits the analytic structure of forecast verification scores to construct a differentiable objective. By backpropagating gradients of this objective from radar fields to the generator, SAPT turns forecast verification into direct training feedback. Across three real-world benchmarks spanning different forecast horizons, AlignPre consistently surpasses state-of-the-art deterministic and generative baselines in forecast skill, demonstrating that aligning generative modeling with domain-specific verification provides an effective paradigm for meteorological forecasting.

Amplitude has always helped teams see how people actually use their products. Its proactive product agent Wave⁠(opens in a new window) helps teams turn those insights into shipped improvements. Amplitude describes Wave as roughly 80% powered by OpenAI models, including GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6 Luna, and GPT‑Image‑2.5 Flare. Wave turns product insights into implementation prepares teams can ship to coding agents, including Codex, then measures the impact.

Amplitude estimates that Wave can help teams ship product improvements in 1–2 days, down from roughly a month. On Amplitude’s own homepage, Wave helped personalize suggestion cards, driving a 160% lift in card-driven sends.

Sources indicate that wave is Amplitude’s proactive product agent. Teams give it a product area and the goals and metrics they want to improve. Wave brings together Amplitude data, session replays, customer feedback, and code to identify and prioritize opportunities, develop solutions, and coordinate implementation with people and coding agents. It then tracks outcomes and uses those learnings to inform the next round of improvements.

Behind that workflow, Amplitude uses different OpenAI models for different tasks. GPT‑6.1 Sol supports the opportunity manager and deep investigations into code and data. GPT‑6 Luna handles frequent, lower-cost tasks such as scanning code and running small evaluation checks. GPT‑Image‑2.5 Flare generates product mockups using screenshots from session replays as visual references.

When an opportunity is ready to build, teams can send it directly from Wave to coding agents, including Codex, with a technical initiative and acceptance criteria to guide implementation.

“The idea with Wave is you have a unified platform with agents that comb through massive amounts of session replays, analytics, and code to find opportunities to improve products,” explains Jacob Newman, Principal AI Product Manager at Amplitude.

Amplitude tested Wave on its own homepage, where generic suggestion cards were meant to help customers start a conversation with an AI agent. Wave discovered that people often bypassed them: in a sample of 100 session replays, 80 users typed their own questions and only 12 selected a suggestion.

Sources indicate that wave proposed personalizing the cards using recent charts, dashboards, or the page a user had come from. It illustrated the change and produced a technical blueprint, including preserving free typing and showing generic suggestions when personalization context was unavailable. After a brief review, the team handed the work to a coding agent and A/B tested the change.

Sources indicate that in the experiment readout Amplitude shared, messages sent through homepage suggestion cards increased 160% relative to control after one day. “It is a great example of how non-groundbreaking things that just get ignored can increase the adoption of features in unexpected ways.” explains Eric Carlson, Senior Principal AI Engineer at Amplitude.

According to recent reports, wave’s tasks place different demands on its models. A deep investigation needs strong reasoning and well-supported conclusions. A small check repeated hundreds of times needs to be fast and inexpensive. Amplitude evaluates quality, latency, and cost for each task, then assigns models accordingly.

In a recent development, for Wave’s Opportunity Investigator, Amplitude evaluated whether models corroborated findings, avoided false positives, incorporated evaluator feedback, recovered from tool failures, and kept claims aligned with evidence. GPT‑6.1 Sol scored 4.06 out of 5 overall, compared with 3.62, 3.52, and 2.94 for three alternative models. It led on all five investigation criteria and had the fastest median investigation time, at 54 minutes.

In a separate evaluation of Wave’s Data Science Agent, GPT‑6.1 Sol scored 67.5 out of 100, compared with 69.3 for another leading model, at a mean model cost of $1.28 versus $2.63 per dispatch. Sources indicate that for high-volume work such as scanning code and running small evaluation checks, Amplitude uses GPT‑6 Luna to keep latency and cost low. Splitting work across specialist agents lets the team reserve more expensive reasoning for the tasks that need it the most.

According to recent reports, for generating wireframes and mockups, OpenAI’s image generation model scored 80.3 out of 100 for solution wireframes, compared with 63.9 for another image generation model. Amplitude’s evaluation covered communication quality, product fidelity, instruction adherence, text and UI legibility, and visual coherence across 15 opportunities.

Customers across industries are already using Wave in beta to identify and ship product improvements. Wave analyzes session and analytics data, then develops recommendations with a proposed fix, technical plan, and acceptance criteria.

From there, teams can control the level of automation. Most teams send bug fixes straight to coding agents, while newly introduced features and bigger bets get a human review.

For changes that reach launch, the path from discovery to execution can be short: among customer-launched experiments, flags, and guides, one in four went live the same day Wave surfaced the opportunity, half in under four days, and two in three within a week.

Industry observers note that jain claims GPT‑6 Astra was 35-40% faster on average than the legacy models Shield had used for computer-use tasks. He also says customer satisfaction is higher on tickets where AI is used, with speed of resolution being a critical factor.

Shield reports faster execution, fewer failures and fewer timeouts. Its teams also spend less time writing detailed instructions to an agent or helping it through a task.

Shield is testing remote-desktop workflows that would let agents perform more complex actions directly on a computer’s desktop.

Jain states, “With GPT‑6 Astra, Forge is now truly an extension of our human technicians.”.

Industry News: Hijacking 3D Generation: Targeted Adversarial Attacks against Image-to-3D Models via Prefix Trajectory Alignment

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (255 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.34075v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Online services that deploy Image-to-3D models enable users to generate high-quality 3D assets from a single image. However, the generated 3D geometry can violate content policies and cause broader security risks. To prevent such content, these services typically use policy-restricted inspectors to examine uploaded images before generation. Since the inspector examines only the visible content of the input, a visually benign image can still induce the generation of policy-restricted 3D geometry. However, turning this vulnerability into an effective attack is non-trivial in the black-box setting: global backpropagation through the long DiT generation trajectory is difficult to fit, while different image preprocessing pipelines across services can substantially reduce transferability. In this paper, we present PTA3D, a targeted adversarial attack against Image-to-3D models that addresses these challenges through Prefix Trajectory Alignment (PTA) and Preprocessing Aware Optimization (PAO). PTA progressively aligns the prefix DiT outputs of the adversarial trajectory with those of the target trajectory, where the core geometric structure is formed, allowing the final geometry to be controlled without optimizing through the complete generation trajectory. PAO exposes adversarial optimization to diverse image transformations rather than a single preprocessing pipeline, reducing sensitivity to the mismatch between surrogate and target services. We establish a prefix-to-output bound and a preprocessing-aware transfer bound to theoretically characterize the effectiveness of the two designs. Experiments on three open-source Image-to-3D models and three online services show that PTA3D achieves 41.5%-88.5% ASR on online services and 90.8%-94.6% ASR in white box settings, substantially outperforming existing attacks.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.34032v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep-learning-generated media are increasingly passed off as real, driving an arms race between image generators and deepfake detectors. Trust in the latter is limited by their often black-box nature; and, while region-based explanations can sometimes be extracted, these become less useful as generation quality improves. Counterfactual examples, which show the minimal change that flips a detector's decision, reveal what evidence drives a verdict, helping analysts decide whether to trust it. This work introduces Counter-DECEIVR (DEtector-guided reCtifiEd flow InVeRsion for counterfactuals), a novel training-free framework that generates counterfactual examples. Counter-DECEIVR steers latents in the velocity field of a rectified flow model using gradients from off-the-shelf deepfake detectors, without training a generator or adapting the detector; unlike prior methods, it requires no per-instance or per-detector fitting and no diffusion training on the target data. It also leverages the detector's explanation maps to concentrate editing to salient regions, turning low-level feature importance into localised counterfactual edits. A single parameter controls the strength of the edits. Across two deepfake detectors and two widely used forensics datasets, Counter-DECEIVR outperforms prior counterfactual generation methods, including training-based ones. Code will be made available upon acceptance.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building trusted agentic payments with networks, banks, and businesses.
  • In a recent development, 1.2B people use ChatGPT each week, and many of them turn to it to research products, compare options, and decide what to buy.
  • To accept payment from ChatGPT Wallet, websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building trusted agentic payments with networks, banks, and businesses.

In a recent development, 1.2B people use ChatGPT each week, and many of them turn to it to research products, compare options, and decide what to buy. With ChatGPT Wallet, we’re now helping people complete purchases, and giving their agents a way to pay that businesses can accept with their existing systems.

To accept payment from ChatGPT Wallet, websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents. We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro owners, so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.

ChatGPT Wallet gives agents a secure way to pay on a user’s behalf. People add a card once, then approve each purchase without re-entering their payment details.

Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

According to recent reports, after the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

It has been revealed that we’re building agent-led commerce to fit reliably into existing systems. Owners keep their card’s existing rewards and protections for eligible disputes with businesses, for example when an item is defective. Banks and networks bring their expertise to evaluating transactions. Users transact directly with businesses, which keep their customer relationships and control over pricing, fulfillment, returns, and customer service.

Over time, we expect consumers to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases with enhanced safeguards that build on today’s protections, including biometric checks and clear records of authorization.

Agentic commerce is still in its early days. As agents begin to take on more shopping and purchasing tasks, many websites and payment systems are still adapting to this modality. Some sites may unintentionally block purchases through ChatGPT Wallet or other agentic payment products, and we are focused on helping businesses make that transition.

Alongside ChatGPT Wallet, we’re publishing a Commerce Partner Playbook⁠(opens in a new window) with tools and practical guidance to help businesses support customers using agents through their existing websites and systems. It covers making product information available, ensuring agent access, and working with payment and risk providers to reduce unnecessary declines. Businesses can start with the areas most relevant to their customers:.

Sources indicate that help customers find accurate product information. Claim your business in ChatGPT and, once verified, revision your business details and upload a product feed with current pricing and availability.

Ensure ChatGPT agents can access your website. Configure your CDN or firewall to recognize signed requests using Web Bot Auth and confirm your general site security measures are not inadvertently blocking ChatGPT agents. Browser access does not require a plugin or product feed.

Sources indicate that work with your payments and risk providers to support agent purchases. Wallet’s payment tokens work with existing checkout flows, but risk systems may still flag legitimate purchases made by agents, leading to declines or cancellations. You can work with your providers to understand how they recognize these transactions. We’re also working with fraud prevention partners including Forter, Riskified, Sardine and Signifyd and payment service providers including Adyen, Checkout.com, and Stripe to help their systems recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.

In a recent development, give agents more ways to work with your business. Build a plugin to let agents check availability, manage carts, or take other actions through your existing systems. Websites can also add WebMCP tools.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.34025v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Due to the Deep Learning requirement for a large training dataset, Transfer Learning has become a central method in the field of Computer Vision, which heavily used Deep Learning. Since the adoption of transfer learning in the field, the performance of the models in computer vision is significantly upgraded. The common transfer learning practice in computer vision research is to use state-of-the-art architectures in the ImageNet dataset as the backbone network. The best performing architecture in ImageNet is at the moment held by EfficientNet, which is a set of architectures that were progressively grown from a baseline architecture. By observing the EfficientNet development approach, it is natural to hypothesize that the smaller EfficientNet architecture is capable to contain the knowledge of the larger architecture. This hypothesis comes from the fact that the larger EfficientNet architecture was grown from the smaller architecture. Therefore, in this study, we experimented if it is beneficial to transfer the knowledge from the larger architecture to the smaller architecture of the EfficientNet. To achieve this goal, we proposed a transfer learning method that uses Knowledge Distillation as the knowledge transfer mechanism from the larger to smaller architecture. We found that the proposed method is able to upgrade the performance of each of the EfficientNet architecture. Several smaller architectures are even able to outperform the larger architecture that was trained using the standard transfer learning method.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we’re starting the OpenAI science blog to give scientists and academic researchers a place to share what they’re discovering with AI and how they’re doing the work. Our mission is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity, and accelerating scientific discovery is one of the most impactful ways we can work toward that goal.

We’ll publish work across a broad range of scientific disciplines, including:.

Research and discoveries: Upcoming scientific results and updates on ongoing research from OpenAI, our collaborators, and the broader scientific community.

Industry observers note that methods and practical guidance: Examples of how scientists use our models for tasks such as scientific computing, data analysis, exploring literature, and planning experiments. We’ll share approaches others can adapt, including how to check the work and where a method falls short.

Industry observers note that perspectives from the scientific community: Firsthand accounts from researchers using AI, what they are learning, and how these capabilities are affecting their disciplines. We’ll also discuss open questions about scientific practice and how to make these tools useful to more people.

It has been revealed that science expands our understanding of the world and makes advances possible, from better medicines to fresh sources of energy. Many of those advances begin with fundamental questions whose practical significance becomes clear only years later.

In recent months, we’ve seen an expanding range of scientific problems our models can address. In September, an internal OpenAI system produced a proof addressing the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem⁠, a longstanding question about the equations describing fluid motion. In early October, we released a broad range of mathematical results⁠. Among them was a result on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis⁠(opens in a fresh window), with a result that gives a tighter bound on the error in a classical formula for estimating how many primes lie below a given number. Later that month, we shared results across mathematics, computer science, and physics⁠ concerning how waves concentrate, the limits of efficient computation, and the mathematical foundations of interacting quantum field theory.

In biology, researchers are using AI to analyze complex datasets, connect findings across fields, and develop fresh hypotheses to test in the lab. Working with PerturbAI and Scripps Research⁠, thousands of agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind analyzed existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells in 32 minutes. By connecting the effects of gene disruptions with scientific literature, they identified possible biological mechanisms for scientists to test. Researchers are also developing their own approaches: César de la Fuente’s team uses ChatGPT and Codex⁠ to build algorithms that identify potential antibiotic molecules, which they then make and test in the lab.

These capabilities bring fresh possibilities and changes to scientific practice. In mathematics, systems that generate proofs raise questions about how new arguments are checked, explained, and incorporated into the field. In experimental sciences, exploring more hypotheses creates opportunities — and challenges — in deciding which experiments to pursue. Across disciplines, researchers are considering what these tools mean for training, attribution, and the skills their work requires. The implications will differ by field, and scientific communities should help shape how these tools are used.

We hope this blog helps more people understand how AI is changing science and how they can use it to explore new questions and make discoveries of their own.

Assessing the Physical Interpretability of AlphaEarth Foundation Embeddings Through Multi-Sensor Satellite Time-Series Benchmarking for Agricultural Mapping

arXiv:2611.34019v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate and dynamic maps of agricultural LULC are notable for agricultural water resource management, particularly in areas where water scarcity is prevalent, such as Morocco. Here, we evaluate the utility of AlphaEarth Foundation Model (AEF) embeddings for agricultural LULC and irrigation-type mapping in Morocco. AEF embeddings were compared to single-date and time-series remote-sensing features using three machine-learning classifiers: XGBoost, CatBoost, and TabPFN. We also evaluated whether AEF embeddings can: (a) provide an efficient and transferable alternative to conventional direct use of Earth observation products and (b) reconstruct biophysical information. Results highlighted that multi-temporal feature time series achieved the highest performance, with accuracies of 0.93 for agricultural LULC and 0.87 for irrigation-type mapping when using TabPFN. However, AEF embeddings yielded comparable results, achieving accuracies of 0.91 for agricultural LULC and 0.85 for irrigation-type mapping, while reducing the need for extensive data processing and manual feature engineering typically required for satellite products. Spatial LULC mapping using TabPFN achieved comparable overall accuracies (0.85-0.86) across the three feature configurations, but revealed substantial differences in mapped tree cover, ranging from 14.57% for surface reflectance to 29.79% for AFE. Physical probing revealed that AEF embeddings strongly encode spectral indices (A30-SWIR: rho=0.58-0.67), (A38-NDMI: rho=-0.72), vegetation (A49-NDVI: rho = 0.72-0.73), and SAR structure (A25-VH: rho = 0.71). Future research should focus on enhancing the interpretability of embedding-based approaches by incorporating physical knowledge to develop more transparent and trustworthy AI systems for agricultural applications.

Evaluating Ukrainian Grammatical Competence in Language Models: Probability Versus Prompting

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (217 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.34016v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Organisations deploying large language models in Ukrainian-language information systems need to know whether a model produces normative Ukrainian. This paper establishes a protocol for measuring that reliably and applies it to 19 models. The instrument is a released set of 1,444 Ukrainian minimal pairs covering the vocative case, numeral-noun and adjective agreement, verb government and calques from russian, with subject-verb agreement as a control; a quarter of the set was checked against the answer key in two independent native-speaker ratings, which agreed at Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.963. Every pair is scored twice: by comparing the probabilities a model assigns to the two sentences, and by asking the model directly, with the sentences presented in both orders so that answer-position effects are measured instead of being absorbed into the score. Three results follow. Order consistency (the share of pairs answered identically when the sentences are exchanged) falls below 0.05 for ten of the nineteen models, and what separates the usable models is instruction tuning, not scale. The vocative case is systematically inverted: 0.153 accuracy against 0.951 on the control, with models preferring the non-normative nominative form of address. Ukrainian adaptation substantially reduces this deficit, measured against the exact checkpoints two adapted models were trained from.

Residual Cross-Model Narrative Convergence under Shared Prompts: Auditing Prompt Controls and Narrative Measurement

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (154 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34015v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stories created by LLMs based on the same prompts can be narratively similar to one another. This similarity may reflect constraints imposed by the prompts as well as the models' writing tendencies. The current research analyzes 51,240 stories created by five models in the StoryScope corpus based on 10,248 common prompts. It uses 213 narrative features in seven dimensions to compare cross-model distances between stories generated from the same prompts with distances between stories generated from different but semantically matched prompts. To assess the relationship between narrative features and prompt content, a semantic relevance mask was evaluated against 420 author-annotated prompt-feature judgments (F1 = .813; near-threshold accuracy = .621). The equally weighted mean Residual Convergence Index (RCI) was .409 without masking and .406 with masking. These findings indicate measurable cross-model narrative convergence relative to a semantically matched-prompt baseline, with little change following semantic relevance masking.
