A step toward defining the Standard Model on a lattice

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in the first guest post on our science blog, physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, describes how he worked with GPT‑6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model.
  • According to recent reports, the Standard Model of particle physics is an extraordinarily successful theory of nature, describing the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces—the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism.
  • It has been revealed that I had a strategy for tackling this problem, but had not been able to prove that it worked in all the cases it needed to cover.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the first guest post on our science blog, physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, describes how he worked with GPT‑6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model. Craig leads the particle theory group at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics.

According to recent reports, the Standard Model of particle physics is an extraordinarily successful theory of nature, describing the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces—the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism. The success of the theory rests on outstanding agreement between theoretical calculations and experiments across eighteen orders of magnitude, from the low energies of hydrogen’s 21-centimeter radio emission to the high energies of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. And yet for all of its successes over the more than fifty years of its existence, a foundational problem remains: how to give the full theory a nonperturbative definition, one that does not rely on treating its interactions as small corrections. In an October preprint⁠(opens in a latest window) prepared with the aid of GPT‑6 Astra, I proposed a candidate definition on a lattice—a grid representing spacetime.

It has been revealed that I had a strategy for tackling this problem, but had not been able to prove that it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. Astra helped turn that strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. To explain what we did, it helps to start with what is missing from our existing description of the Standard Model.

What does it mean to say that we lack a definition of the Standard Model? Quantum mechanics and special relativity tell us how the particles and forces of the Standard Model interact. Unfortunately, we don’t yet know how to make complete predictions based directly on these interactions. Instead, we often start by imagining that the interactions are turned off, so that electrons would no longer repel each other. We can solve that problem exactly, then put the interactions back in as a series of small corrections. When the corrections get progressively smaller, a few terms can give a remarkably precise answer—for example, it has allowed physicists to predict the strength of the electron’s magnetism to within a few parts in a trillion. This approach is known as perturbation theory.

However, much of the richness of the Standard Model lies outside the realm of perturbation theory. Take the mass of the proton: the proton is made up of three quarks, but its mass comes primarily from the motion and interactions of the quarks and the strong force-carrying gluons inside it. If you turn off the strong force, the proton falls apart entirely, so perturbation theory is not a useful guide to understanding the size of the proton’s mass. More powerful methods are needed to access information about the theory nonperturbatively, where the interactions are present from the start and not treated as small corrections.

For the full Standard Model in continuous spacetime, we don’t have a nonperturbative definition, or even an understanding of whether the interacting theory is mathematically well defined. A promising alternative is to discretize spacetime into a grid of points, known as a lattice. The spacing of the grid defines the shortest distance our theory can resolve, and studying a finite grid allows us to give a rigorous nonperturbative definition of the theory at a given spacing. It also enables us to put the theory on a computer, where we can calculate its predictions directly without resorting to perturbation theory. This approach, known as lattice field theory, has led to remarkable progress in our understanding of the strong force over the last few decades, including a quantitative understanding of the mass of the proton from first principles.

If lattice field theory has been so successful for the strong force, why haven’t we extended it to a nonperturbative lattice definition of the entire Standard Model? Here a crucial difference stands in the way: the Standard Model is an example of what is known as a chiral theory.

Sources indicate that A chiral theory is one that looks different under reflection in space. Think of gloves in a mirror: the mirror image of a left-handed glove is a right-handed glove. If you have one of each kind, the mirror image does as well, so your collection of gloves looks the same under reflection in space. But if you only have a left-handed glove, the right-handed glove in the mirror is different.

Recent findings suggest that this notion of handedness extends to many of the fundamental particles in the Standard Model, known as fermions, including quarks and electrons. Most forces in the Standard Model are not chiral: the strong force and electromagnetism, for example, treat left-handed and right-handed fermions in the same way. Such theories can be put on a lattice more readily.

Sources indicate that but the third fundamental force of the Standard Model, the weak force, lacks this reflection symmetry. It treats left- and right-handed fermions differently, and so does not look the same under mirror reflections that exchange left and right. This treating of different-handed particles differently is what makes the Standard Model a chiral theory. And it turns out that putting chiral theories on a lattice is profoundly challenging. If we try to put a left-handed fermion on the lattice, the most natural rules give you a right-handed partner you never asked for. This is a surprising outcome, which we’ll unpack momentarily. Whatever the reason, this means a straightforward lattice formulation of the Standard Model gives the wrong particle content for the weak force. Doubling is one reason a complete nonperturbative definition of the Standard Model has been missing since the theory took shape.

Recent findings suggest that to understand doubling, consider an analogy with light. Light has two polarizations, which describe the orientation of the electric field as the light moves through space. (This is familiar if you wear polarized sunglasses, which block the horizontally-polarized light that reflects off water or roads while letting through vertically-polarized light.) Although polarized sunglasses pick out a basis of horizontal and vertical polarizations, for our analogy it will be more useful to pick a basis where these two polarizations are left-circular and right-circular, meaning that the electric field is rotating either clockwise or counterclockwise around the direction of motion. As we’ve noted, electromagnetism is reflection-symmetric, so its actual laws are the same for both left-circular and right-circular polarizations. (For the technically inclined, left and right refer to chirality when we talk about fermions. In our analogy with light, they refer to the photon’s helicity, which tells us whether its spin points along or against its direction of travel.).

Industry observers note that but imagine you wanted to emulate a world with only left-circular light, akin to the way the weak interactions single out left-handed fermions. To study this in the lab, you could put a laser producing left-circular light into a box with a mirror at either end. The light could build up as it bounced back and forth, allowing you to study it carefully—kind of like putting the Standard Model on a lattice. In each case you are bounding the accessible length scales of the theory to gain control—the lattice bounds the shortest accessible distances, while the box bounds the longest distances.

In a recent development, if you built the box using ordinary mirrors (like putting a chiral theory on the lattice in the most straightforward way), you’d be in for a surprise: the left-circular light coming out of the laser becomes right-circular when it bounces off the mirror at the other end, so now the box contains both polarizations of light. This occurs because the mirror reverses the direction of the light without changing how the electric field is rotating (as seen from the same end of the box), which flips the polarization. This is a bit like the appearance of doublers when you put a left-handed fermion on the lattice. You supplied only left-handed light, and the box supplied the other hand.

There is a clever fix. You can make a chiral mirror using special films whose molecules line up in layers. The alignment turns a little from one layer to the next, tracing a spiral down into the film. For light whose wavelength and handedness match the spiral, the small reflections from different layers reinforce one another, flipping the rotation of the electric field in the light that bounces back. The film sends left-handed light back left-handed and lets right-handed light pass through. Such chiral mirrors have been around for more than a decade, and the phenomenon even occurs in nature: some scarab beetles have a similar spiral in their shiny shells. If you constructed your box using chiral mirrors, then the light traveling in both directions would be left-circular.

According to recent reports, A similar trick works on the lattice: decades ago, Paul Ginsparg and Nobel laureate Ken Wilson1 worked out the lattice rules analogous to the requirement that chiral mirrors reverse the rotation of the electric field upon reflection. Rajamani Narayanan and Herbert Neuberger2 built the analog of the chiral mirrors by finding the necessary definition of fundamental particles on the lattice, known as overlap fermions. Finally, Martin Lüscher3 showed how to tell the difference between left-handed and right-handed overlap fermions on the lattice, while Yoshio Kikukawa4 and collaborators explored how this might be used to describe weak interactions in the Standard Model. However, one piece was still missing.

To identify that piece, let’s come back to our box with chiral mirrors. The circular polarization of light tells us which way the electric field turns as light propagates, but there’s another notable property of the light in our experiment: the optical phase. Imagine water waves rolling past the pilings of a dock, and watch the water rise and fall at one piling. The wave’s phase is the stage of that rise and fall you catch it in when you look, perhaps just past its highest point and on its way down. For our circularly polarized light, the optical phase tracks the same kind of cycle at a fixed spot in the beam, with the electric field pointing up at the “crest” and down at the “trough.”.

Industry observers note that the relative phase of two waves determines how much they add or cancel at the same point. At one piling of a dock, two waves arriving in phase lift the water higher as their crests meet, while a crest arriving with a trough can leave the water close to its usual level. Similarly, light with the same phase in the same place builds up, while light with different phases can cancel out. In our box with chiral mirrors, left-circular light is now bouncing back and forth inside the box. After a lap, the returning light meets fresh light from the laser going in the same direction. If their electric fields are in step, they reinforce and the light builds up inside the box. If the fields are half a cycle apart, they point in opposite directions and the returning light cancels some of the fresh light. To build up a strong beam, we want the phase of each return to arrive in step with the source.

In a recent development, to get the phase right, we can rotate one chiral mirror relative to the other. Imagine a mark at twelve o’clock on the rim, and spin the mirror about the beam as though the beam were its axle. Moving the mark to three o’clock turns every layer of the film by a quarter turn and shifts the phase of the reflected light by half a cycle. We can set the angle to make up for the phase accumulated on the rest of the trip. Once the returning light arrives in step with the laser, we have a splendid laboratory for studying purely left-handed light.

Imagine changing the force fields until they return to where they started. The orange arcs show the phase the left-handed fermions pick up on that round trip, first on the original grid and then on finer ones. Each bracket pairs two neighboring grids. Adding up the differences between their arcs recovers the phase shift on the original grid. The teal arrow undoes that shift, bringing the fermion measure back to its starting phase.

On the lattice, overlap fermions give us a way of keeping only the left-handed fermions that we want, and getting rid of the doublers. But this doesn’t tell us how to set the phase. (The phase in question is quite different from the one we’ve encountered in our chiral mirror thought experiment, but the analogy is good.) On the lattice, this becomes tricky because the phase depends on what the forces of the Standard Model are doing at every grid point. Lüscher worked out the phase prescription for a simpler class of theories such as a chiral version of electromagnetism, but the alignment for the full Standard Model remained open for more than 25 years.

We can try to assign a phase by starting with one configuration of forces on the lattice and following the allowed left-handed fermions as we change the force fields in small steps. Now take a series of steps that bring the force fields back to where they started. The same states are allowed at the end, yet the way we carried them around the loop can leave us with a different phase. In the box, we adjusted the mirror to compensate for the phase the light picked up on a lap. On the lattice we have to work out how to compensate for the phase picked up around every loop.

In a recent development, my idea was to take the force fields on the grid where we want to define the theory and represent those same fields on a succession of finer grids. Comparing the allowed fermion states on two successive grids tells us one part of the phase correction for a small change in the forces. Adding up those parts gives us the phase rule on the original grid. The proof shows that it gives the right correction around every allowed loop. The correction for a change at one spot depends mainly on the fields nearby, and different mathematical descriptions of the same fields give the same answer. This supplies the measure for the Standard Model at finite lattice spacing, under a bound on field strengths at the scale of the grid.

Developing this refinement strategy into a proof required several rounds of work with Astra and discussions with outside experts. GPT‑6 Astra was essential to turning the refinement idea into a working construction. It suggested the right way to carry a given set of force fields onto finer grids, revealed that the comparisons on finer grids would converge to a definite answer, and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. Human experts also played a key role; lattice field theorists Maarten Golterman, Andreas Kronfeld, and Yigal Shamir graciously spent time looking over Astra’s proof and asking probing questions that helped me to build confidence in the result. Their experience with the problem and the questions they asked were invaluable as the construction took shape.

It has been revealed that the result is a candidate nonperturbative lattice definition for the Standard Model, potentially answering a question that had been open for more than fifty years. As with all scientific progress, however, this construction is much more a beginning than an end. Scientific dialogue among experts is required to decide if this prescription has all the properties we desire. The method that Astra and I proposed is far more an answer in principle than an answer in practice; much work lies ahead to make it useful for realistic lattice simulations. Right now I’m thinking a lot about whether this construction satisfies reflection positivity at finite lattice spacing, a condition that helps connect calculations in this lattice model to a quantum theory in which probabilities are conserved.

The construction also leaves open the question of defining the interacting theory in continuous spacetime. OpenAI’s recent proof of the existence of Yang-Mills theory (of which the strong and weak forces of the Standard Model are examples) provides the missing puzzle piece. This enabled them to prove the existence of the simplest unified Yang-Mills theory that includes the gauge fields and fermions of the Standard Model by starting with overlap fermions on the lattice and taking the continuum limit. I’m optimistic these developments will lead to newly introduced progress in our understanding of the Standard Model.

Industry observers note that P. H. Ginsparg and K. G. Wilson, “A remnant of chiral symmetry on the lattice⁠(opens in a new window)”, Phys. Rev. D 25, 2649 (1982).

R. Narayanan and H. Neuberger, “Chiral determinant as an overlap of two vacua⁠(opens in a latest window)”, Nucl. Phys. B 412, 574–606 (1994).

Recent findings suggest that M. Lüscher, “Abelian chiral gauge theories on the lattice with exact gauge invariance⁠(opens in a fresh window),” §2.4, Nucl. Phys. B 549, 295–334 (1999).

The mechanism combines semi-relaxed optimal transport to adapt cluster capacities to the underlying data, a competition loss to concentrate mass onto well-supported cluster prototypes, thereby starving degenerate ones, and hard pruning to progressively eliminate them. Extensive experiments on five public benchmarks demonstrate that CARROT achieves state-of-the-art NMI and ARI, accurately recovers the number of clusters without supervision, and faithfully preserves size-imbalanced community structures.

arXiv:2611.34008v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large collections of three-dimensional radiation dose maps linked to patient anatomy are needed to develop artificial intelligence (AI) models for personalized internal dosimetry in nuclear medicine, but access to such data remains limited. Here we present DosePET, an open-source dataset of 2,100 patient-specific absorbed-dose maps generated by Monte Carlo simulation of publicly available PET/CT examinations: 1,503 [18F]FDG examinations from ENHANCE.PET and 369 [18F]PSMA-1007 and 228 [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 examinations from PSMA-PET-CT-Lesions, acquired at five institutions with seven scanner models. For each examination, the CT was resampled to the native PET grid to build a voxelized patient phantom, the quantitative PET image defined the radionuclide source, and radiation transport was simulated with GATE version 9.4. Organ and tissue masks were generated from the CT with TotalSegmentator. Each study folder contains a NIfTI dose map integrated from scan time to infinity, 117 binary organ/tissue masks, a report of regional dosimetric quantities, including mean absorbed doses, dose conversion factors and scan-time dose rates, and simulation metadata. The total processing time was 1,542.4 hours. Python tools support selective downloading and conversion to scan-time dose-rate or dose-per-decay maps, and an agent skill guides pairing with the source PET/CT images. DosePET is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/eltzanis/DosePET.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dots deliver launch reports unprompted, flag challenges people might miss, and talk through upcoming meetings on the commute to work.

The day after Holiday Extras⁠(opens in a latest window) introduced a new feature in its app, Liam Thompson, the company’s VP of AI Innovation, got a report on how it was performing. He hadn’t asked for one. His dot, which he calls Beast, noticed the launch, pulled data from Google BigQuery via the ChatGPT plugin, and brought him the results.

Industry observers note that holiday Extras is a UK travel technology organization that helps travelers book the practicalities around a trip, from airport parking and hotels to lounges and transfers. Its promise is simple: less hassle, more holiday.

In a recent development, the promise of simplicity extends to employees too. ChatGPT Enterprise gives them a foundation for using AI, Codex helps them turn their expertise into working software and better customer experiences, and dots⁠ simplify all the work in between.

Liam and his colleague David Lee, Director of Innovation & Growth, shared how they use their dots as assistants and thought partners: to talk through what’s ahead, catch challenges they might miss, and do work that would otherwise wait until they got back to their desks.

Industry observers note that david named his dot Brian and he calls him on his morning commute. They talk through the meetings ahead, and David can ask Brian to run a report using connected tech giant data. “By the time I get into the office and sit at my desk, the report is there and it’s ready to go,” he says.

When some API keys needed to be retired, Brian flagged the matter, went back through David’s email, and surfaced a list of people who might be affected. David could see who might need a heads-up without having to reconstruct it from old threads.

Recent findings suggest that “My dot is my orchestrator of everything,” says Liam. Beast reminds him about replies he hasn’t sent and finds answers from past conversations. Instead of scrolling through his chat history, Liam can ask Beast when they talked about something and what the answer was.

“It relaxes me having Beast there, because I know that if I miss something, he’s probably already covered it, and he is keeping an eye on all the things that are going on,” says Liam.

Liam had tried two other assistants, OpenClaw and Hermes, but claims he wasn’t comfortable giving them much information. “With anything OpenAI in our firm environment, I know I can trust it,” he says. He gave Beast access to his Slack, inbox, Drive, and laptop, which made it more useful to him.

Liam talks with Beast for his morning and evening briefings. “Voice is my favorite. Bidirectional voice is the game changer for interaction with OpenAI,” he says. “It’s like having a natural conversation. I spend at least two hours a day in a voice conversation with Beast.”.

Sources indicate that dots are also a design partner. Liam, who trained as a designer, turned to Beast to animate 3D characters for an app he was working on. He gave Beast access to After Effects and Rive on his laptop, and then watched it work.

Sources indicate that beast animated the characters and put them in the app. Liam says the job would have taken him several days; he estimates Beast did it in about ten minutes. “I went to university for three years to learn design,” says Liam. Watching Beast work, he thought, “Well, it’s done a better job than me.”.

For Holiday Extras, the next opportunity is to help more people put their dot to work. David wants the people experimenting with dots to share what they’re learning, helping others see what’s possible and try it for themselves. The next idea could come from anyone, whether they start with preparing for a meeting, building something, or making everyday life a little easier.

That builds on the ambition behind the organization’s work with OpenAI: giving people across the business the confidence and tools to work differently and helping useful discoveries spread.

According to recent reports, for anyone getting started, Liam’s advice is to simply create a dot and start a conversation. “There’s no excuse not to get started. Really, just go.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The upcoming partnership will help young people build AI skills for the future workforce, prioritizing those not in education or employment.

The King’s Trust⁠(opens in a latest window) has unveiled a major partnership with OpenAI designed to help up to 25,000 young people build AI skills for work, prioritizing those not in education, employment or training.

OpenAI is making a £1m donation to the youth charity to support this work.

This is part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications that The Trust will launch in the coming months, designed to help young people stay ahead of a changing labor market.

The announcement comes as The King’s Trust marks its 50th year and looks to the future, helping ensure young people are supported to succeed in an increasingly AI-enabled world.

The King’s Trust and OpenAI have launched a £1 million partnership to help young people across the UK build AI skills for work, prioritizing those who are not in education, employment or training (NEET). The program aims to support up to 25,000 young people over the next 18 months, helping them develop practical skills and confidence to move toward education and employment in an AI-enabled economy.

It has been revealed that the program will help address a gap in young people’s experience of AI while responding to their appetite to learn. The Open University’s Business Barometer 2026⁠(opens in a new window) found that 68% of 16–24-year-olds surveyed who were not in education, employment or training would be willing to train or upskill to improve their job prospects.

The partnership will help prepare young people for the opportunities and challenges of a rapidly changing world of work by combining opportunities to learn AI skills with recognized qualifications and practical experience. It forms part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications being developed by The King’s Trust, designed to equip young people with the skills employers need as AI transforms the world of work.

Working with employers, AI specialists and young people, The King’s Trust is exploring the skills young people will need in a world of work where AI is becoming part of everyday life, and how these can complement the employability skills already embedded across its programs.

Building on a 50-year legacy of supporting more than 1.3 million young people, The King’s Trust wants to ensure the next generation gains the skills and confidence needed to thrive in an AI-enabled economy.

Ahead of the final report of the independent Young People and Work review, the Rt Hon Alan Milburn welcomed the partnership, reflecting on the shared ambition to improve young people’s opportunities to learn and earn.

For OpenAI, the partnership forms part of a broader commitment to helping young people develop the skills and confidence to benefit from AI. It builds on wider efforts to make practical AI learning more accessible, including through OpenAI Academy, which provides free learning resources for students, job-seekers and other learners.

arXiv:2611.33972v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can a classifier computed in closed form on a frozen encoder match gradient fine-tuning? We present closed-form weight-space programming (WSP): a large language model (LLM), used as a design assistant, writes programs that read a frozen masked language model through cloze-style prompt templates at several layers, fit closed-form heads (shrinkage discriminant analysis, kernel ridge regression and the encoder's label-word prior) on labelled data, and select among a pool of candidate heads by cross-fitting. No gradient is computed and no encoder weight changes. We instantiate the framework on RoBERTa-large. On 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 training labels, WSP is ahead of full fine-tuning (FT) and LoRA at every label budget (by 0.3 to 0.6 points on average; the registered non-inferiority tests pass) and within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning (PFT); these datasets also shaped the recipe. With fewer labels its lead over FT and LoRA grows: 1.2 to 3.5 points with 64 and 128 labels, and 3.8 to 5.3 points in the few-shot setting of 16 labels per class, where WSP is again within half a point of PFT on the development datasets. On six held-out datasets, WSP stays ahead of LoRA and within half a point of FT on average, although with six datasets no registered test passes, and PFT is ahead, by 1.30 points with 8,192 labels. WSP never collapses and is deterministic, but it needs one encoder pass per template (17 here). We report all eight recipe versions, every decision that saw test results, and 27 ideas that did not help.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.33961v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Classical dimensional analysis defines admissible dimensionless representations but does not determine which combinations capture the dominant physical dependence, whether it changes across physical regimes, or when dependent-variable rescaling is required. We present AI Buckingham, an agentic framework for autonomous dimensionless discovery from natural-language descriptions of physical problems and observational data. It couples reasoning and planning by a large language model (LLM) with predefined symbolic and numerical tools. Literature-based knowledge retrieval supports dimensional checking, gradient-based clustering identifies physical regimes, and mutual information provides an objective, reparameterization-invariant criterion for identifying dominant dimensionless groups. Explicit numerical criteria determine the group count and assess simplification. Across ten physical systems spanning fluid dynamics, magnetohydrodynamics, thermal convection and additive manufacturing, AI Buckingham recovers established similarity representations and resolves regime-dependent scalings. For the longstanding challenge of predicting turbulent drag on rough surfaces, it identifies informative reparameterizations of surface statistics that improve equivalent sand-grain roughness estimates for engineering-oriented drag modelling.

RefMix: Expanding Endpoint Proposals for Diversity-Preserving Reward Fine-Tuning

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (167 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.33957v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Online forward matching aligns flow-based generative models by repeatedly generating, rewarding, and fitting model-produced endpoints. However, this behavior creates an on-policy feedback loop: as high-reward modes become increasingly favored, alternative modes become less likely to appear in subsequent training pools, progressively reducing visual diversity. We introduce RefMix, a reference-assisted endpoint proposal strategy that addresses this limitation by injecting alternative candidates into the training pool while retaining the original task reward and forward matching objective. In particular, RefMix uses a reference model during early high-noise steps to expose alternative visual modes, followed by the current reward-tuned model for endpoint completion. Across state-of-the-art online forward matching methods, RefMix consistently improves visual diversity while preserving task reward performance. Controlled inference experiments further demonstrate that training-time endpoint exposure is critical to improve reward--diversity trade-offs, beyond the impact of reference-assisted inference. By rethinking how training endpoints are proposed, RefMix achieves up to 44% higher diversity over forward matching baselines at comparable reward levels.

Introducing computer-use agents, a latest healthcare model configuration, and new healthcare plugins that work across healthcare software to get real work done.

Healthcare teams need to piece together information from the EHR, hospital policies, scheduling systems, and payer portals to deliver care and manage operations. With ChatGPT for Healthcare, we’re bringing the tools teams already use and the medical evidence they need into one platform to help them spend less time navigating systems and more time caring for patients.

Today, we’re sharing advances in computer use that help AI agents carry out multi-step work across existing healthcare software. We’re also improving how trusted clinical search finds, evaluates, and cites medical evidence. A new healthcare model configuration in the Responses API lets developers build trusted clinical search into their own applications. And we’re expanding our healthcare plugin ecosystem with more than 20 new plugins.

Together, these capabilities help healthcare teams find the information they need, make decisions grounded in medical evidence, and carry out next steps across the systems they already use.

It has been revealed that organizations often need to move information between disconnected systems to prepare documentation, coordinate care, and complete administrative tasks. Computer-use agents can help with these steps by navigating the software that teams already use: reading screens, clicking, typing, and moving between applications.

Today, we’re sharing advances in computer-use agents for healthcare, including more capable, safe, and affordable models for clinical and administrative workflows, and access controls and audit logs for secure deployments. We’re also sharing our work with healthcare organizations that are deploying agents, including Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health, to process referrals, move documents between systems, and bring together the information care teams need. In the demo below, a clinician uses Voice in the ChatGPT app to ask for help following up on an MRI request. The agent reviews the chart and drafts an order and patient reply for review.

According to recent reports, healthcare organizations can start with a workflow that spans existing applications, set which applications agents can access, and establish clear controls for which steps require human review. To support HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information, organizations must use eligible services covered by their BAA with OpenAI, apply required security and retention settings, and extend protections to connected systems. Content shared with ChatGPT for Healthcare is not used to train models.

Read more about our computer use research, customer stories, and demonstrations in Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams⁠.

Industry observers note that we’re improving trusted clinical search in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians, including how ChatGPT finds, evaluates, and cites medical evidence. These updates help clinicians connect relevant evidence to clinical questions and translate it into practical next steps, with citations they can inspect.

To measure the impact of these updates, in a blind evaluation, physicians reviewed responses to real-world clinical questions across multiple specialties, including multi-turn conversations. In over 1300 reviews, physicians rated the updated experience more highly across all eight dimensions evaluated, including factual correctness, safety, actionability, and source authoritativeness.

It has been revealed that developers can now bring cited medical evidence into their applications with a healthcare configuration of select OpenAI models, including GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. Available through the Responses API today, the configuration pairs the models with a harness tailored to clinical questions and trusted clinical search.

In a recent development, GPT‑6.2 Astra with the healthcare configuration ranked first among the systems we evaluated on HealthBench Professional, a benchmark of 525 challenging tasks written by physicians to test how well AI can answer questions about patient care, draft clinical documentation, and synthesize medical evidence. It earned a length-adjusted score of 74.4%, 6.3 percentage points ahead of the highest-scoring non-OpenAI system, Claude Fable 5.2 with web search.

All model configurations have web search enabled and are evaluated at their highest reasoning effort.

In a recent development, during a visit, clinicians rely on rapid point-of-care responses. On HealthBench Professional, GPT‑6.2 Astra configured for healthcare delivered higher-quality responses in an average of 23 seconds, compared with nearly three minutes for the same model using general-purpose web search even when using its highest reasoning setting.

According to recent reports, for developers deploying these tools at scale, cost per response matters too. In a separate comparison on the same benchmark, Astra with the healthcare configuration scored higher than Claude Fable 5.2 with web search at less than half the API cost per scored response ($1.37 vs. $2.90), with both systems at their highest reasoning settings.

Customers are already seeing the value of building with the new model configuration.

Sources indicate that the healthcare configuration builds on the API’s existing privacy and data controls. Organizations can support HIPAA-compliant workflows with an applicable Business Associate Agreement with OpenAI.

These plugins let teams bring more of their work into the same conversation: reviewing patient records and hospital protocols, preparing prescriptions for clinician review, coordinating patient outreach, checking insurance eligibility, and analyzing healthcare costs and operational performance.

DuoMI: Dual Mutual Information Regularization for Expert Reuse in Looped Transformers

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (179 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33952v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce Dual Mutual Information Regularization (DuoMI), a method for regulating expert routing across rounds in looped mixture-of-experts (MoE) Transformers. When two rounds of computation share an expert pool, their routers may favor different expert subsets, limiting the reuse of individual expert parameters across rounds. Even when aggregate expert usage is identical across rounds, we would still prefer each token to retain some experts while switching to others. DuoMI addresses both aspects of routing: it uses round-level marginal mutual information to limit the dependence of aggregate expert usage on the round, and token-level conditional mutual information to penalize average cross-round routing changes that fall outside a target interval. During training, DuoMI computes differentiable penalties from soft routing distributions over all experts. It adds no model parameters and leaves sparse Top-$k$ routing strategy unchanged at inference. On a looped OLMoE backbone in which paired adjacent layers share experts, DuoMI improves the average score across $15$ downstream tasks from $50.08\%$ to $51.82\%$, a gain of $1.74$ percentage points over the looped baseline.

InstructTTS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Objective Instruction-Following TTS

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (282 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.33937v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Instruction-following text-to-speech (Instruct-TTS) renders a target transcript in the manner described by a free-form natural-language instruction, and a good rendition must succeed on three fronts at once: following the instruction, pronouncing the transcript correctly, and sounding natural. Reinforcement learning has become the standard way to post-train such generative models toward human preferences, and TTS systems increasingly adopt it. When the three objectives are optimized together under a single scalar reward, typically with group relative policy optimization (GRPO), training tends to be unstable: the objectives compete, and the shared enhancement drifts toward whichever one is easiest to improve, producing a seesaw among them. We instead adapt on-policy distillation (OPD), which fuses several single-objective teachers by matching their velocity fields on the student's own rollouts. Realizing this for Instruct-TTS first calls for a sound reward on each axis, which we analyze carefully: a distilled Qwen-Omni proxy for the costly Gemini judge, dialect-free data for the WER reward, and DNSMOS in place of the language-biased UTMOS. We then train three single-objective teachers with GRPO and fuse them with OPD, routing each rollout to the instruction-following or WER teacher by its data domain and letting every rollout additionally follow the MOS teacher for quality. This lets instruction following and intelligibility improve together without a trade-off, but the quality target conflicts with instruction following, so following it additively reintroduces the seesaw. We therefore propose conflict-aware velocity fusion, which projects the quality target off the direction that opposes the primary objective before fusing, and show that it markedly reduces the instruction-following/quality trade-off. The fused model improves over scalar-reward GRPO on all three objectives at once.

We investigate a complementary paradigm that uses full-spherical perception to follow designated targets without active heading adjustment. To support this setting, we introduce 360UAV-ETrack, a simulation benchmark comprising 2,652 sequences, over 1.73 million synchronized observations, eight tracking tasks, and 150 held-out closed-loop scenarios. We propose 360UAV-TVLA, a panoramic vision--language--action (VLA) framework integrating persistent visual referring (PVR), compressed temporal memory (CTM), and geometry-aligned trajectory supervision (GTS) for instance identification, motion reasoning, and three-dimensional control. Experiments across two VLA backbones show consistent gains over standard fine-tuning, with normalized average tracking frames increasing from 22.56\% to 35.28\% for $\pi_0$ and from 25.68\% to 33.64\% for $\pi_{0.5}$. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Healthcare is fragmented, and teams often need to move information between systems manually before a patient can get care.
  • Recent findings suggest that computer-use agents carry out multi-step workflows by clicking, typing, and moving between applications.
  • Industry observers note that today, we’re sharing upcoming results measuring model performance, safety, and cost in clinical and administrative workflows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Healthcare is fragmented, and teams often need to move information between systems manually before a patient can get care. When a clinician recommends an MRI, for example, the information an insurer needs may be in a patient’s medical record, but a team member still needs to retrieve it and enter it into a separate portal to complete an authorization request.

Recent findings suggest that computer-use agents carry out multi-step workflows by clicking, typing, and moving between applications. In healthcare, this enables AI to help with repetitive workflows in the software teams already use.

Industry observers note that today, we’re sharing upcoming results measuring model performance, safety, and cost in clinical and administrative workflows. We’re also sharing the ways we’re working with leading healthcare organizations like Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health to advance and apply computer use, across authorization requests, referrals, discharge planning, and outreach between visits.

Industry observers note that healthcare teams, developers, and individual clinicians can access these capabilities today through the OpenAI API, ChatGPT for Healthcare, and ChatGPT for Clinicians. Organizations can support HIPAA-compliant workflows, configure approvals and agent access, and record audit logs for secure deployments.

To show how a computer-use agent can help a clinician and an authorization specialist work on the same MRI request, we built a demo using synthetic patient data. A patient messages their clinician about lower back pain. A computer-use agent reviews the patient’s visit notes, physical therapy records, and prior imaging in the EHR. It drafts an MRI order, an encounter note, and a reply to the patient for the clinician to review. The agent then uses the same records to prepare a prior authorization request in the insurer’s portal for an authorization specialist to review.

It has been revealed that we evaluated GPT‑6 Astra on tasks clinicians handle in their EHR inboxes. These tasks, shaped by physician input, require Astra to carry out multi-step workflows designed to test both clinical reasoning over longitudinal patient context and navigation of complex interfaces. Reviewers examined the model’s actions alongside the notes, orders, and patient messages it produced, assessing whether the work would be helpful and clinically safe in the context of the task.

Clinical safety was assessed by evaluating whether inaccuracies, omissions, or actions in the model’s work could plausibly lead to patient harm. Overall, 99% of 325 reviewed tasks were rated safe. Physicians rated helpfulness on a five-point scale, selecting “very helpful” or “extremely helpful” in 93% of 646 assessments.

We also evaluated computer-use agents for administrative tasks, such as prior authorizations, appeals, and medical equipment orders. On HealthAdminBench⁠(opens in a fresh window), an independent benchmark from Stanford researchers measuring performance on common administrative workflows, GPT‑6 Astra earned 94.3% of available rubric points, while GPT‑6 Luna earned 91.8%, despite costing 98% less at 8.5 cents per task. Both models were evaluated at maximum reasoning effort. These results show progress toward capable, affordable agents for high-volume administrative workflows.

Our partners build software used in hundreds of health systems, coordinate care for members globally, and deliver care to hundreds of millions of patients. The following examples showcase how organizations are developing, piloting, and deploying computer-use applications to save time, solve critical problems, and improve patient care.

Recent findings suggest that CVS Health is using OpenAI’s computer-use capabilities to automate repetitive work across clinical systems, including sending documents, processing referrals, and supporting specialist consults. The agents navigate existing applications to complete steps that APIs do not fully support.

In one production workflow, an agent cleared a months-long document-sending backlog over a weekend. Another handles the system steps for tens of thousands of consults each day, helping team members focus on work that needs their expertise. CVS Health uses validation checks and human oversight, with screenshots and action records to verify actions and application state. CVS Health is open sourcing its Agent Kit⁠(opens in a fresh window), built with OpenAI’s Agents SDK, which packages this approach as a repeatable process for broader use.

It has been revealed that data remains within the CVS Health enterprise-controlled infrastructure, governed by their enterprise AI Governance team and established responsible AI policies. Production data is not used to train foundation models.

Sources indicate that abridge is developing computer-use agents to help clinicians carry out care aims across use cases and applications they use daily, including those without APIs. Their planned inpatient use case builds on the clinical conversation, adding EHR information and nurse and clinician context to identify what needs attention and to coordinate next steps.

For example, a clinician can ask the Abridge Assistant to help resolve a patient’s discharge barriers. Agents can work concurrently on medication access and home-health coordination, using computer interaction alongside calls and messages. The clinician stays focused on the patient and is brought in for decisions requiring clinical judgment.

Learn more⁠(opens in a new window).

Sources indicate that as part of The Cigna Group’s broader collaboration with OpenAI, Cigna Healthcare is using OpenAI’s frontier models alongside its own clinical expertise to bring together relevant information across systems and give care teams more complete context about each member’s needs and experience. That can include information about benefits and coverage, providers, appointments and prior interactions, helping care teams better support members around care plans established by their treating providers.

Previously, Cigna Healthcare case managers had to navigate more than 10 separate clinical and administrative systems to gather this context. Computer use can now help navigate these systems and bring relevant information together in seconds, reducing the time spent searching for information – ultimately giving case managers more time to support members.

It has been revealed that computer use lets agents complete tasks in EHRs and payer portals that APIs don’t reach. In healthcare, that capability is only usable if every action is controlled and auditable. Ambience built additional controls to support that oversight.

In a recent development, in this demonstration, Ambience uses evidence from the patient’s chart to prepare a prior-authorization request on an insurer’s website. When the record is ambiguous, the agent stops and asks the clinician, then waits for approval before submitting. Health systems set which actions the agent can take, can pause it at any point, and get a step-by-step log for audit.

Recent findings suggest that healthcare startups are helping turn advances in computer use into new ways to support care teams. These five companies are combining AI agents with healthcare expertise to help teams navigate systems, coordinate next steps, and move care forward.

Computer-use agents in healthcare require evaluating clinical safety, protecting patient information, and setting clear limits on what agents can do without human review.

It has been revealed that chatGPT for Healthcare provides role-based access controls and audit logs to support oversight. Organizations can build additional review and approval steps into their workflows and configure the applications and environments agents use to limit access to the records and actions needed for each task. Organization data is not used to train OpenAI foundation models.

To support HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information, organizations must use eligible services covered by their Business Associate Agreement with OpenAI and the required security and retention settings.

Computer-use agents for healthcare are available today in ChatGPT for Healthcare, ChatGPT for Clinicians, and the OpenAI API. Here’s how healthcare organizations, clinicians, and developers can get started.

Healthcare organizations: Contact our sales team⁠ to discuss using AI in your clinical and administrative workflows. Existing customers can ask their workspace administrator to enable computer use in ChatGPT Work and Codex.

Developers: Build healthcare applications with the OpenAI API⁠(opens in a fresh window), and explore our computer use guide⁠(opens in a new window) to build agents that work across existing software.

We hope these advances enable healthcare teams to spend less time moving information through systems and more time caring for patients.

arXiv:2611.33926v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper describes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server through which a general-purpose AI agent operates a discrete element engine, commercial or open-source, while the simulation runs. The agent submits a long simulation to the engine and, while it computes, reads the running model, changes it, or stops it. The human modeler stays at the engine's console and graphical interface throughout, and the agent sees what the modeler does there. The tools are derived from what the agent needs to do at the engine and are held to four principles: correctness, coverage, orthogonality and simplicity. Two documentation tools let the agent search the engine's manual and browse it level by level. Five execution tools let the agent run code in the engine, submit long simulations in the background, check on them, read the running model, and stop them. A bridge inside the engine serves these tools in a commercial DEM engine, PFC, and an open-source one, YADE. In a case study, a general-purpose agent calibrated a drained triaxial model of dense Toyoura sand against laboratory data in both engines, while the modeler worked at the same engine; the agent noticed the modeler's actions at the console and acted on them. The same calibration on YADE was then given to seven language models, three sessions each and without human intervention. Twenty of the twenty-one sessions reached the targets, and nineteen of the parameter sets lie in one small region of the admissible ranges. The server and the bridge are released as two open-source packages, itasca-mcp, which also serves FLAC, 3DEC, MPoint and MassFlow, and yade-mcp.

Industry News: Beyond the Happy Path: Generalizing Robot World Models from Simulated Failures

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (262 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.33925v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robot world models are increasingly used to evaluate and plan policies, yet robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations. Off the happy path, when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or slips, their predictions break down. Across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than that of a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two models are worse than this baseline. We present WorldReforge, which teaches world models what happens when manipulation goes wrong. We construct the Reforge dataset of 62k simulated trajectories by perturbing reference grasps in position, orientation, and closure timing, recording each resulting push, slip, or failed pickup with ground-truth object pose, contact, and surface points. WorldReforge turns this ground truth into two training signals without additional inference cost. Interaction Alignment focuses reconstruction on the small object and contact regions that a global loss underweights, and Surface Correspondence trains backbone features to follow the same physical surface points across frames. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on unseen objects, and it lowers the error in predicting how two actions' outcomes diverge by 43.3%. Although trained only in simulation, it also improves reconstruction on DROID and on real failure videos. Controlled data studies show that failed contact and successful holding teach complementary physics: failed contact teaches how objects respond, and holding teaches how a grasped state persists. Our code, data, and models are available at aim-uofa.github.io/WorldReforge/.

Industry News: Our first phase of embedded assessments

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We have signed agreements with four independent assessors—Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire—for our first phase of embedded assessments.
  • Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases.
  • Our initial assessments focus on alignment and safeguards for models during training and internal use, complementing our safety cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We have signed agreements with four independent assessors—Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire—for our first phase of embedded assessments. As AI capabilities advance rapidly and the potential risks grow, public reporting from independent assessments can give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing those risks.

Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases. Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated.

Our initial assessments focus on alignment and safeguards for models during training and internal use, complementing our safety cases. They build on our priorities and principles for third party assessments and years of work with third party evaluators, including a recent pilot assessment of our internal monitoring systems⁠(opens in a latest window) with deep internal access and an investigation of the Hugging Face incident⁠(opens in a new window). We’ll use what we learn to deepen our work with independent experts in the coming months. These efforts also support our commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where we agreed to independent assessments of our safety controls. These collaborations can contribute to stronger shared standards for independent assessment and public transparency across the industry.

It has been revealed that in this pilot assessment, Apollo Research⁠(opens in a fresh window) will assess whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior. Drawing on evidence from training, safety testing, and internal use. Apollo will assess four claims in two stages:.

Training did not incentivize subversion.

Strong evaluations and red teaming do not elicit subversion.

Models have not attempted subversion during internal use.

Reasoning behind subversion would be detectable.

For the first stage of Apollo’s assessment, we’ll provide access to selected public and unreleased models and training checkpoints, relevant training data and evaluation results, training intervention records, monitoring systems and flagged behaviors, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

Goodfire⁠(opens in a new window) will embed interpretability researchers and use the Goodfire platform to analyze model internals. The main objective of their assessment is training run monitoring, debugging, and alignment. The primary audience for their assessments are internal OpenAI researchers, who will use their findings to make safety improvements. Goodfire will also publish learnings and findings as the collaboration progresses.

We intend to conduct two assessments with METR⁠(opens in a new window), focused on model alignment and monitoring:.

In a recent development, alignment assessment: For the first phase, METR will assess misaligned behavior in our largest reinforcement learning run to date, including failures that our existing tests and monitors may have missed. Within the selected run and agreed access, resources, and safety arrangements, METR would independently set assessment priorities and iterate on searches, analyses, and elicitation experiments. Access will include sampling relevant checkpoints, training and eval rollouts, and misalignment monitoring records for this run. For this first phase, the assessment will focus on our largest frontier RL run.1.

Monitor assessment: We recently worked with METR to conduct a monitor stress testing exercise2. We have preliminarily agreed to conduct another monitor assessment⁠(opens in a new window) which we intend to be broader, but this is pending mutual agreement on the assessment scope.

Transluce⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) will conduct an initial assessment of our post-training alignment evaluations, examining their quality and coverage. For the initial assessment, we will provide Transluce with access to selected public and unreleased models, our post-training alignment evaluations and relevant results, supporting model behavior data and safety case documentation, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

OpenAI and Transluce also share the intent to conduct a follow-on assessment of approximately eight weeks in early 2027, with broader access to additional models, deeper access to our alignment evaluations, and information on how evaluation results inform model release decisions.

We’ve developed protocols and processes with input from the assessors to balance deep access with security, confidentiality, oversight, and the independence and integrity of assessments. We are sharing them to shed light on how we will work with embedded assessors, and to advance discussion about norms for embedded assessments, which have yet to be standardized. We expect that these will need to evolve as we learn more about how to best conduct these assessments. Especially in the early stages of embedded assessments, we expect technical access challenges, space constraints, evolving security protocols, and other unexpected concerns to arise. We hope to work through these challenges collaboratively with our embedded assessors and share lessons learned.

In a recent development, each engagement begins with an agreed scope and the access, resources, and safety arrangements needed to conduct a rigorous assessment. Some assessments test specific safety claims; others give assessors room to discover unexpected failure modes within a defined system or training run. In both cases, assessors need the freedom to follow evidence, refine their methods, and propose further assessments when findings warrant it. We also have a process for addressing additional access needs as assessments develop. When direct access could expose our most sensitive IP, such as model weights or architecture, we will consider alternatives, including pairing assessors with OpenAI researchers to run analyses.

According to recent reports, assessors who need access to sensitive confidential information will work on site at OpenAI offices and be provided OpenAI devices to conduct their work. The primary purpose is to protect the security of the information they access. Working onsite also gives assessors the opportunity to engage with dedicated staff who can help them navigate their access and provide context for their assessments. We also expect our embedded assessors to follow at minimum3 the same security standards as OpenAI employees when running experiments and evaluations.

Our Safety and Security Committee (SSC), an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board, will have visibility into the embedded assessment and the ability to exercise their oversight responsibilities before, during, and at their conclusion. They will receive unredacted reports, and both the assessors and the SSC will be able to speak with each other during the assessment, including privately. Disagreements among OpenAI and any evaluator will be escalated to the Safety Advisory Group and OpenAI executives, who will have a specified time period to resolve them, and the SSC will be notified of any such disagreements promptly when escalated. If a disagreement remains, the matter will be referred to the SSC for resolution.

Discussions with employees help assessors understand internal information and the context behind the work. OpenAI will authorize and provide guidance to staff members who can speak to assessors, and assessors may request additional staff to speak with as needed. To encourage open, candid conversations and protect the privacy of our staff, these discussions are off the record, meaning that they can inform the assessments but cannot be published or attributed to employees. Through a separate attestation pathway, assessors can request OpenAI-attested statements verifying, correcting, or clarifying something they learned in conversation with employees. These statements are not attributed to individuals or intended to characterize individual views. Assessors may publish statements that OpenAI attests to, or disclose that OpenAI declined to attest to a statement.

Recent findings suggest that managing conflicts of interest clearly and transparently—including those involving personal relationships, financial interests4, and other challenges—is notable to the integrity and independence of evaluations. Cool-off periods5 also need to be designed carefully, so assessors can work responsibly across labs while handling competitive information sensitively. We are working with our assessors to develop clear processes for both conflicts and cool-off periods, including allowing for flexibility in mitigations and transparency in decisions to request recusal.

In a recent development, assessors maintain independence in publishing their assessments, but we will retain the right to redact confidential information, consistent with our previous third-party engagements. We may also request responsible disclosure delays to allow time to act on findings that could pose security or safety risks and remediate complications that remain.

Public reporting will help people understand the findings and their limitations, while more detailed confidential reports give oversight bodies the evidence they need to act. We want these assessments to improve how we identify and address risks, and give the public a clearer basis for judging our safety work.

These assessments bring an independent perspective to our ongoing alignment and safety work. Public reporting on their findings will make that work more transparent and provide greater assurance about how risks are being identified and addressed. We expect this first phase of assessments to lead to longer-term, consistent embedded engagements over time that can continuously provide third party safety signals and recommended improvements on our most load bearing safety claims and safety cases.

Sources indicate that we’ll continue working with multiple independent third parties to help build a healthy assessment ecosystem with diverse expertise and approaches. Some investigations need sustained, on-site work with sensitive systems; others primarily evaluate deployed or soon to be deployed models or review public documentation.

Sources indicate that in the coming months, we’ll support external assessments across a broader range of safety questions. We are also exploring future embedded assessments that would examine compliance with our safety frameworks, as well as our organizational culture and processes. We are committed to expanding this work and helping build the capacity and shared standards needed to sustain it.

This scope is less expansive than what METR outlines in their alignment assessment proposal⁠(opens in a latest window), which envisions a broad survey of misalignment.

Sources indicate that we recently conducted a 3 week long monitor red teaming exercise with METR, which granted them access to our codebase, monitors, relevant trajectories, and discussions with OpenAI research staff for the purpose of better understanding our monitors. https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-22-red-teaming-openai-agent-monitoring/⁠(opens in a latest window).

In some cases, there will be more stringent standards applied depending on the conditions of the experiment to allow for careful security vetting.

Recent findings suggest that apollo Research and Goodfire accept financial compensation for their work, but their compensation is not contingent on the results of their assessment. METR and Transluce do not accept financial compensation for their assessments, but may accept API credits / compute to use within their assessments. We do not believe that accepting financial compensation prevents assessors from maintaining independence - but we believe it is important to disclose this.

We ask staff at third party organizations who participate in an embedded assessment to observe a brief cool-off period before embedding with another AI developer, to reduce the risk of inadvertent disclosure of confidential information.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.33919v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing methods for adapting autoregressive (AR) language models to diffusion generation focus mainly on full-attention architectures. More efficient hybrid architectures remain underexplored. We introduce DiCALM, a recipe for converting the hybrid convolution-attention models of the LFM2 family (LFM2 and LFM2.5) from AR to masked-diffusion generation. DiCALM progressively extends LFM2's causal gated convolution so that it captures local context in both directions. It combines this extension with a masking warm-up and joint AR--diffusion training. In controlled experiments, DiCALM performs comparably to the corresponding fine-tuned LFM2.5-based AR models and delivers consistent speedups over them at both the 350M and 1.2B scales: over 1.4x on average and up to 1.79x.

Correlation-Aware Evidential Fusion for Trusted Multi-View Classification

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (202 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.33900v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Trusted multi-view classification aims to make accurate and reliable predictions by integrating information from multiple views. Existing methods typically estimate class evidence and uncertainty for each view and combine the resulting opinions through aggregation rules. However, they generally treat different views as independent information sources, overlooking the correlations among them. Highly correlated views tend to produce similar evidence, and treating them as independent sources may repeatedly count consistent information and give it disproportionate influence, while weakening complementary evidence that provides additional information. Consequently, such correlation-unaware fusion may not only limit classification performance but also produce miscalibrated uncertainty estimates. To address this issue, we propose Correlation-Aware Fusion of Evidence (CAFE), a framework for trusted multi-view classification. CAFE applies complementarity-based trust discounting to the evidence produced by view-private experts and introduces a correlation-aware constraint to reduce the repeated contribution of similar evidence. It then learns sample-specific weights from the global multi-view context to adaptively combine the correlation-adjusted private evidence with cross-view collaborative evidence. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that CAFE consistently improves classification and calibration performance in general settings, with particularly significant gains when strong correlations exist among views.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (284 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.33893v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM-based coding agents are increasingly used for long-horizon tasks such as building an entire program from a specification. Products like Codex and Claude Code let an agent delegate work to parallel subagents, multiplying run cost, yet it remains unclear whether and when delegation produces a better program. We compare a single agent with a main agent delegating to subagents on repository-construction tasks from NL2Repo and ProgramBench (which also provides an executable reference program). We compare scores at equal time and equal cost, run intervention experiments, and analyze fine-grained behavior. On randomly drawn tasks, parallel subagents raise hidden-test pass rates by only about 1 to 5 percentage points at up to 3.8x the cost of a single agent. Their gain is larger on hard tasks, where we find evidence of three mechanisms. Self-checking: with GPT-5.6 Sol, one sentence telling a single agent to probe the reference program first recovers most of this gain at a fraction of the cost; from GPT-5.6 Sol to GPT-6.1 Sol, the gain shrinks as single agents check their own work more. Fresh context: in extended runs, a single agent that periodically starts a upcoming session with an empty conversation makes faster early progress in every comparison than one that resumes its conversation. Modularity: multi-agent runs produce more modular code (more files and shorter functions), closer to the upstream source. We observe similar patterns in a smaller replication with Opus 5.5 on Claude Code. Overall, subagents help when (i) a single agent stops checking too early, (ii) a long session keeps editing with little improvement, or (iii) modular code helps on the task; otherwise, they mainly add cost.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This news was originally shared by LVMH’s Media Division and can be read here⁠(opens in a fresh window).

It has been revealed that paris, 16 November 2026—LVMH Group’s Media Division and OpenAI announce the signing of a strategic agreement to support newly introduced uses of artificial intelligence across all the division’s publications and make their journalism more accessible through ChatGPT. The agreement includes the deployment of OpenAI tools and ChatGPT Enterprise to teams across the media division, enabling them to develop AI applications tailored to their day-to-day work.

Their shared ambition is to empower teams across the media division to experiment with and develop practical uses of AI that support journalism and high-quality reporting.

Artificial intelligence is a powerful tool that, when put to work in newsrooms, enables journalists to focus on the core of their profession: investigating, analysing and writing. Teams will be able to explore applications such as document research, document comparison and preliminary translation. The goal is to enable them to devote more time to investigative reporting, analysis and reporting in the field.

In addition, in an increasingly crowded information landscape, personalisation has become a major priority. Artificial intelligence is an essential tool for developing and delivering products and services that meet the needs of customers, readers and advertisers alike, helping to attract and retain them and grow revenue across the publications.

This partnership is a tech giant-wide initiative that also enhances the presence of content from LVMH Group’s Media Division in ChatGPT, providing summaries and excerpts in response to relevant user questions, identifying their sources and including direct links to the original articles. The partnership will extend across all the division’s publications and support the evolution of roles throughout the organisation: streamlining operations, improving efficiency, and encouraging innovation and creativity to prepare today’s publications for tomorrow. The rollout will be supported by training tailored to everyone’s use cases.

LVMH Group’s media division, Groupe Les Echos-Le Parisien, brings together 17 media brands covering news, finance, culture, heritage, arts and music. With 1,800 employees, including nearly 700 journalists, it reaches more than 27 million people in France every month.

The Group’s media brands: Boursier.com⁠(opens in a new window), Capital Finance, Challenges, Connaissance des Arts, Historia, Investir, La Lettre de l’Expansion, L’Agefi, Le Parisien, Aujourd’hui en France, Les Echos, L’Opinion, medici.tv⁠(opens in a new window), Mezzo, Mieux Vivre Votre Argent, Paris Match, Radio Classique.

The Group’s exhibitions and publishing houses: Citadelles & Mazenod, Fine Arts Paris, In Fine, Salon du Dessin.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (225 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33875v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Nearest-neighbor methods are local, simple, and interpretable, but their non-parametric form makes them memory-intensive, expensive at inference, and difficult to integrate into differentiable neural architectures. We introduce Random Voronoi Networks (RVNs), a family of structured three-layer MLPs that express nearest-neighbor geometry through sampled Voronoi comparisons. The first layer computes Random Voronoi Features (RVF) from affine pairwise separators between selected training samples, the second layer aggregates these comparisons into Voronoi cells or top-k neighborhood scores, and the readout layer produces classification or regression predictions. We show that, when all samples and pairwise comparisons are included, step RVNs recover exact Euclidean k-NN, while ReLU RVNs provide a violation-score realization for 1-NN that can be relaxed into a differentiable soft weighting. Subsampling yields approximate RVNs with explicit control over the number of cells and features. We study several unsupervised sampling methods that trade off random coverage, directional diversity, coordinate sparsity, and empirical feature variance. Empirically, RVFs produce a highly effective data encoding strategy, providing performance boosts to downstream methods ranging from linear to modern tabular deep learning models. Finally, we showcase that RVF provides an interpretable feature map due to its k-NN based construction and ties to pairwise local directions. These results position our Random Voronoi formulation as a bridge between nearest-neighbor rules, random features, and modern tabular models.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.33850v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Random Network Distillation (RND) is a scalable novelty signal for RL based on a fixed random target network and a trained predictor. However, it can overgeneralize: the predictor extrapolates the random target off the data manifold, causing novelty scores to collapse on unfamiliar inputs. This paper analyzes this failure through a kernel-theoretic lens. Under a GP target model and an NTK-regime predictor, we show that the RND novelty score is a cross-kernel residual variance: it is governed jointly by the target covariance kernel and the predictor NTK, rather than by either one alone. This identifies overgeneralization as spectral under-excitation. Motivated by this view, we formulate spectral target design as a principle for shaping RND novelty geometry. As a concrete instance, we replace the implicit random-network target with a bandwidth-controlled Random Fourier Feature (RFF) target, redistributing residual signal toward modes less attenuated by the predictor. Experiments on offline D4RL, online Atari, and Fetch manipulation benchmarks show improved novelty discrimination and downstream RL performance. The code for the RL implementation is available at https://github.com/tuuktuc86/RFF-RND.

FEAST: Fair and Efficient Adaptive Sampling for Task-Free On-Policy Learning

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (198 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
