arXiv:2611.33827v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language agents trained from self-generated experience must allocate a limited rollout budget across heterogeneous capabilities. A common strategy is to prioritize capabilities with strong current learning signals, but in on-policy learning these signals are endogenous: past allocation changes the policy and therefore the evidence available for future allocation. This can create a feedback loop in which under-trained capabilities receive increasingly fewer opportunities to improve. We formalize this effect through the Quota-Efficiency Law (QEL), which reveals that allocation history can change learning efficiency even under matched capability-specific exposure. Motivated by this, we introduce FEAST, a task-free adaptive sampling framework that separates opportunity allocation from compute allocation. FEAST dynamically discovers capability clusters while preserving their learning histories, maintains continued sampling opportunities across clusters, and reserves a rollout budget for each selected cluster. Within each budget, it progressively concentrates computation on prompts with informative reward variation. Across GURU-18K and SMC, FEAST improves average performance over competitive adaptive sampling baselines under matched rollout budgets, while better preserving learning progress on weaker capabilities. Ablation studies further support the complementary roles of cross-cluster opportunity protection and within-cluster selective allocation. Code will be released upon acceptance.

How Revolut raises ambition without lowering the bar

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With OpenAI models and Codex, Revolut is giving its teams more room to solve complex problems—from software engineering to financial crime.
  • Reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge.
  • To turn seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With OpenAI models and Codex, Revolut is giving its teams more room to solve complex problems—from software engineering to financial crime.

Reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge.

To turn seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context.

Saved on security code review with Codex.

Revolut⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) was built to challenge the way people interact with money. That ambition now stretches across more than 40 markets, 800,000 businesses and a consumer base that’s grown by 23% in the last 12 months.

Add to that a manufacturer culture that expects small, lean teams to move quickly and it’s no surprise that ChatGPT and Codex have proven a natural fit.

“The perfect description for a high-caliber Revolut person is someone who can identify a problem really swiftly, deduce the solution, design four scenarios, identify the best one of those four then take it to market,” claims Kim Maniovich, Revolut’s Global Head of Business Marketing.

“Partnering with OpenAI enables us to build a lot of these solutions in a way that’s incredibly lean, cost-efficient and really tailored to the unique way that we work.”.

In a recent development, but moving faster is only part of the opportunity. For Revolut, the bigger question is what becomes possible when talented people spend less time on the mechanics of getting things done—and more time tackling problems that could fundamentally change financial services.

As Revolut grows, so does the complexity of protecting its customers. According to one report⁠(opens in a fresh window), over half of adults worldwide reported a scam encounter in 2025.

For Revolut, every transaction creates another opportunity to identify suspicious activity, investigate potential risks and implement robust and tailored protections for its customers. But the sheer volume of those transactions far outstrips the human resources available to any bank.

In a recent development, “The biggest problem we can tackle with AI today is the scaling of humans versus the demand that we get,” says AI Lead David Abitbol. That’s why one of Revolut’s largest AI applications is a FinCrime agent powered by OpenAI models.

Rather than requiring investigators to work through every eligible case manually, the agent can examine information, apply Revolut’s rules and complete the defined process automatically.

The release of GPT‑5.5 was a turning point. It was then, states Abitbol, that the models had become capable and cost-effective enough for Revolut to delegate screening and investigation workflows entirely to the agent. The result is greater capacity to monitor transactions without increasing investigator headcount at the same rate as demand.

That, adds Information Security Engineer Mo Amiri, “translates directly into stronger protection and a more resilient system our customers can trust.”.

According to recent reports, ‘Move fast but build trust’ could easily be Revolut’s internal engineering slogan. While Abitbol points out that Codex has delivered a 30-60% reduction in coding time, he’s also clear that certain guardrails are non-negotiable.

Industry observers note that “We have a systematic framework where anyone in the tech giant who’s building anything with AI has the same set of standards across development, A/B testing, and business metric prediction,” he says. “So every engineer is held to the same standard of quality across the company. We started to get enough intelligence for reasonable costs where we could increasingly delegate initial investigations and screenings to the agent.”.

For Senior Platform Engineer Dmitry Pitik, that 30-60% reduction in coding time became tangible while he was building an internal code-review service. He designed the system, broke it into features and initially assumed he’d need a development team to implement it.

Recent findings suggest that “I realised I don’t need a whole team of developers to implement this,” he recalls. “I can just launch different agents and assign each of them a particular task.” Codex became his implementation team, while Dmitry spent more time designing the system, planning the work and reviewing what came back.

This is a pattern that Abitbol has seen across Revolut. As Codex returns capacity to engineers they’re using that reclaimed time “to spend more time discussing design and the best solution. So we spend more time designing instead of implementing.”.

That doesn’t remove the need for engineering expertise, it just changes where that expertise is applied. “Every developer is responsible for the code they produce, and we don’t blindly trust AI,” Pitik says. The result is a different division of work: AI can help with implementation, while engineers devote more attention to the decisions that determine whether the software is useful, reliable and worth building.

Recent findings suggest that that overhead is worth it. As Codex works on one task, Pitik can work in parallel on another. That kind of multitasking is essential in a company where, as Kim Maniovich explains, the average employee has “three different jobs.” Using Codex creates a virtuous (if challenging) flywheel where “month on month the targets we’re setting get more aggressive, but also more attainable. And so the bar keeps moving up. AI is making that possible.”.

Examples of what Revolut has been able to do with this upcoming-found capacity include developing a tool to build web UIs for internal apps and external-facing products.

Or turning seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context in a single day, creating a foundation for tools intended to help designers work more effectively. The exercise illustrates how AI can make accumulated organisational knowledge more accessible, reducing the effort required to work with complex systems. “We can shift focus from the things which are crucial but hard to do without AI to the things which matter for customers,” claims Senior Designer Dmytro Pavlov.

According to recent reports, mo Amiri’s job is to make sure all of this speed is matched by security—not just for customers but for Revolut’s own employees. That gives him two views of AI at once: how it can help Revolut investigate a problem, and what teams need before they can deploy it safely.

Recent findings suggest that in a phishing investigation, for example, an analyst once had to gather an email, inspect its links and attachments, trace the sender and assemble the evidence manually. “With stronger AI tools, we can uncover those connections instantly, and dig deeper into the questions that really matter,” he indicates.

While AI does the legwork and presents an investigator with a structured case, it’s still down to the individual to review the original records, decide whether the explanation makes sense and approve any action.

Amiri applies the same thinking when teams bring fresh AI applications into Revolut. He follows the complete chain: what information the system sees, where that information goes, which tools it can reach, what it can do with that access and what happens when something fails. He also tests whether apparently convincing conclusions are actually supported by the evidence.

It has been revealed that “The most critical decision is always about accountability,” he indicates. “If an AI tool suggests a code change, a human engineer needs to understand that change well enough to stand by it. That directly drives how we design the review process, giving developers the context they need without cluttering their everyday workflow.”.

Industry observers note that for Revolut, safeguards aren’t separate from innovation. They help establish the conditions under which teams can confidently adopt more capable technology. “That’s how you earn real confidence in AI,” he explains, “by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go.”.

30–60% reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge.

One engineer built an internal code-review service by delegating implementation tasks to multiple Codex agents.

One day to transform existing design-system documentation developed over roughly seven years into AI-readable context.

One to two days saved on one substantial security code-review task.

More transactions screened through the FinCrime agent without scaling investigators one for one.

Start with a problem worth solving. Revolut has put AI to work where demand is growing fastest and the stakes for customers are highest.

Use speed to raise ambition, not lower standards. Time saved on coding and investigation creates room for better design, harder questions and more consequential work.

Sources indicate that keep people on the hook. AI can gather evidence, write code and recommend action. A person still needs to understand the work well enough to stand behind it.

Build trust before you scale. Be clear about what a system can see, what it can do and what happens when it fails—then test those decisions as you go.

Make your knowledge usable. AI works better when it can reach clear, well-organised context. The same exercise often shows where the organisation itself needs to be clearer.

In a recent development, revolut has already shown how AI can increase the amount and complexity of work its teams can attempt. Its next opportunity is to carry that combination of capability, judgment and design into the way customers interact with their money.

Abitbol imagines a more conversational interface in which customers can ask Revolut to help with everyday financial tasks: blocking a card, managing a subscription or finding ways to save for a trip. Pavlov sees the design challenge underneath that experience—turning complexity into something consistent, familiar and easy to use.

According to recent reports, kim Maniovich connects that future to the culture driving the work. “I hope that we can take the values that we operate by every day—this unapologetic ambition, the desire to never settle—and enable people to apply that to their own lives through the products that we build for them.”.

As AI makes it easier to build, the differentiator becomes knowing what to build—and maintaining the judgment, standards and customer understanding to do it well. For Revolut, that’s the bigger promise of intelligence at work: less time spent on the mechanics of getting things done, and more capacity to make financial services safer, simpler and more useful for everyone.Banking services provided by licensed Revolut Group entities. Pitfalls of Dependency-Ready Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (238 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.33823v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have shown strong performance on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku, Trip Planning, and Countdown. MDMs introduce a freedom in the order in which tokens may be unmasked, and to exercise this freedom for good accuracy, early decoding strategies relied on signals of confidence or the downstream impact of decoding a token. However, simple examples seem to illustrate that resolving a token's dependencies before unmasking it should be notable. Therefore, we examine whether this principle, which we call dependency-ready decoding, would contribute to better accuracy, from a practical and a theoretical perspective. We examine a recent decoder that implements dependency-readiness through attention, and generally find that when it performs better than confidence-based or future utility baselines, its decoding order collapses to left-to-right decoding. For theoretical analysis, we establish a definition of dependency without resorting to attention, measured by an information-theoretic score of how much revealing a single masked token (or a set) would shift the model's prediction for another. We prove that when the margin is large relative to this score, no such revelation can change the top prediction, so in this regime Maximum-Margin decoding already commits dependency-ready tokens. These findings leave only a narrow scope for future dependency-ready decoders: their potential benefit is limited to positions with margins smaller than the information-theoretic sensitivity, and reliance on attention should be questioned.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.33812v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: RNA inverse design seeks nucleotide sequences that fold into specified target structures. Existing methods rely on learned generators that can miss exact structural matches, especially beyond their training distributions, or on costly search over a vast, multimodal sequence space. Search is further complicated by globally coupled nucleotide interactions, as correcting one pairing error can create new errors beyond a fixed repair scope. To address this, we introduce KnitNet, an inference-time scaling framework that learns from verifier feedback to refine sequences for exact fold-back matching. Starting from candidates generated for a target secondary structure, KnitNet uses mismatched folds to infer nucleotide dependencies and adapt its joint repair strategy, while an online surrogate learns to predict which edits are promising. This makes search progressively more informed and compute-efficient. Crucially, KnitNet generalizes across RNA structural regimes by changing only the optimization signal to match the verifier required by each setting. Across five secondary-structure benchmarks, KnitNet increases exact solve rates by an average of 21 percentage points over continued sampling with 70% less time-to-solve. On OpenKnot57 specifically, KnitNet is the first method to achieve exact computational matches for all complex, pseudoknotted structures. Beyond 2D, KnitNet improves 3D structural self-consistency over per-target RL by 7.8% while being 39.3% faster, demonstrating generalization and effective inference-time scaling across RNA design regimes.

arXiv:2611.33806v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep learning models often struggle with sharp local optima and overfitting in limited-data regimes, and exhibit limited capacity for capturing high-order, complex probability distributions. Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models, by operating in exponentially large Hilbert spaces, can efficiently represent such distributions and provide favorable inductive biases for learning, offering a promising pathway to overcome these limitations. However, their practical deployment in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era is severely hindered by gradient coupling, barren plateaus, data-loading bottlenecks, and high inference latency. To bridge classical AI and QML, we propose QPAT (QCBM-Prior-Assisted Training), a universal framework that employs a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) as a learnable generative prior to provide a task-aligned structured inductive bias during classical model training. The framework can be seamlessly integrated into any classical backbone, including LSTMs, CNNs, and Transformers. We introduce a decoupled fitness-based scoring mechanism and a stochastic "Drop-Prior" mechanism to implicitly distill quantum structural knowledge into the classical weights during training. Evaluated extensively on six benchmarks spanning time-series forecasting, computer vision, and natural language processing, our framework consistently outperforms purely classical backbones in both predictive performance and stability across random seeds; ablation studies further show that these gains are not reproduced by unstructured random priors or a classically learned generative prior. Remarkably, our approach enables completely classical inference, bypassing quantum latency while preserving quantum-enhanced accuracy, paving a highly practical path for QML deployment.

Sources indicate that how more than 1,800 scientists used ChatGPT—and what they expect AI to mean for scientific discovery. Explore the findings in our fresh report.

Scientific progress depends on researchers asking upcoming questions and finding ways to answer them. AI is becoming part of that work, but we’re still learning where it helps and what it could mean for discovery.

OpenAI’s Economic Research team studied more than 580,000 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists in the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers summer pilot and surveyed 251 participants.

Scientists used ChatGPT across the research process, from reviewing literature to analyzing evidence and developing ideas. Surveyed participants estimated that the same work, at the same quality, would have taken 1.9 times as long without AI. And 98% of those who answered our question about discovery timelines expected AI to accelerate discovery in their field.

Recent findings suggest that by default, OpenAI does not use participants’ data from the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to train its models. To protect researchers’ privacy, we used tools called automated classifiers to sort messages by the type of research activity, such as reviewing literature, writing code, or analyzing data. The research team could see those categories, but did not read the underlying messages or ChatGPT’s responses.

We studied how scientists used ChatGPT across the research process.

According to recent reports, for each scientist, we calculated the share of their scientific messages in each activity, then averaged those shares, giving every scientist equal weight. Percentages are rounded; other research activities accounted for less than 1%.

Industry observers note that scientists in this study used ChatGPT to explore ideas, analyze evidence, write code, and communicate their findings. Their responses also point to ambitions beyond saving time: finding more promising questions and pursuing a wider range of research.

According to recent reports, understanding whether those expectations translate into faster discovery will take more research. Progress will also depend on the funding, staff, and experimental capacity scientists need to test their ideas.

We want to empower more scientists to explore what AI can make possible in their work. Alongside this research, we’re expanding ChatGPT for Academic Researchers⁠, with free access for more than 200,000 researchers around the world. Helping scientists turn their ideas into discoveries that improve lives is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

arXiv:2611.33793v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) seeks collision-free paths for multiple agents from their start locations to their goal locations while minimizing path costs. Most MAPF algorithms assume that each agent occupies a single vertex and that the actions of all agents are synchronized. These assumptions may limit the use of MAPF planners in practice. Existing planners that get rid of both assumptions either handle only a few agents or cannot improve their solutions. Recently, a planner called LSRP* was proposed, which is scalable and anytime with asynchronous actions, but still limited by that each agent occupies a single vertex. This paper develops a latest planner called LSRP*-LA for MAPF for large agents with asynchronous actions (LA-MAPF-AA), where an agent can occupy several cells. LSRP*-LA is scalable and complete, and it keeps improving solution quality after the initial solution is obtained until the runtime budget depletes. We analyze the properties of LSRP*-LA and test it against several baselines with up to 800 agents on various maps. LSRP*-LA can handle twice as many agents as baseline methods and its solution cost is about half that of recent synchronous planners for large agents.

Industry News: Triage Before Fine-Tuning: Feasibility-Gated Selection and Monitored Adaptation of Embodied Foundation Models for a Fixed Physical Platform

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (326 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.33772v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Embodied foundation models are increasingly deployed by selection: a practitioner picks a public checkpoint by benchmark rank and fine-tunes it on local data. The platform is fixed before the model is chosen, with little or no local data. We ask what such a checkpoint loses on a fixed platform and which part of the loss local data can buy back. We split the gap by what can repair it. A sensing gap, information the sensors do not capture, cannot be closed with their data; a latency gap, output arriving after the control loop needs it, belongs to the loop, not the weights; only a distribution gap is fine-tuning's to repair. TRIAGE turns this into feasibility-gated selection and monitored adaptation in five stages: gates on the sensor contract and on end-to-end latency that no score can override, probes on ten minutes of local logs, a ranking by target-relevant score among the candidates that pass, and fine-tuning that is monitored and checked in closed loop before release. On driving benchmarks, a deadline below a leading closed-loop model's latency makes it collide on 80 to 90% of routes, and losing field of view moves plans 2.2 to 5.7 times more than losing resolution at equal pixels. Local frames close 75% of a stability gap but raise perturbation sensitivity at small budgets, and picking by score violates a gate in two of four deployment profiles. On a full-scale vehicle, the factory camera failed the sensing gate and an added camera repaired it. The latency gate removed the two highest-scoring candidates, neither of which completed a closed-loop trip. The selected model passed acceptance in 4 of 5 closed-loop trips, and the closed-loop check withheld a fine-tuned model that had improved offline. TRIAGE lets organizations that cannot train foundation models from scratch find out whether a public checkpoint can run on the robot or vehicle they own, and what to fix if not.

Breaking: ScanAR: Parallel Row-Scan Decoding for Efficient Image Generation in Unified Autoregressive Models

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (263 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33761v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Unified multimodal autoregressive (AR) models represent text and images in one token sequence and generate all modalities with a shared next-token prediction head. Their image generation, however, decodes an $H\times W$ visual grid token by token in raster order, which takes $HW$ sequential steps and dominates inference time. Existing acceleration methods for visual AR generation either change the tokenizer, the prediction head, or the model interface, or keep the model but cannot reach high parallelism without losing quality, so they do not carry over to unified AR models. We propose ScanAR, a row-scan parallel decoding method that only redefines the predecessors of visual tokens. The first visual row is generated from left to right as usual, and each later row is generated in a single parallel step, with every token predicted from the vertically aligned token of the previous row. Nonvisual tokens keep the standard autoregressive rule. ScanAR reduces the visual decoding depth from $HW$ to $H+W$ without changing the backbone, vocabulary, or output head and without adding parameters, and it supports both training from scratch and lightweight post-training. On Emu3.5-Image-34B, ScanAR post-training reaches a GenEval score of 82.36, the best among post-training acceleration methods trained on the same data, and generates $512\times512$ images $13.8\times$ faster than raster decoding under the same inference setting. On ImageNet, ScanAR trained from scratch has the highest throughput at every model size with FID comparable to raster LlamaGen. On the 34B Xiaomi-Robotics-U0 model, ScanAR preserves the overall quality of embodied scene generation, interleaved image-text generation, and video generation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.

Today, we’re releasing a new tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), interventions that interrupt harmful behavior and point people toward help, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators. These efforts build on our Child Safety Blueprint and our ongoing work to detect, block, and report abuse. For parents, the goal is simple: technology that helps keep children safe, with people in control.

It is well⁠(opens in a fresh window) established⁠(opens in a new window) that combatting online child predators requires coordination across many organizations. Individual companies like OpenAI have a responsibility to prevent our technology from being exploited by predators to harm children, and we also must work together with the broader industry, child safety organizations and law enforcement to advance our collective efforts to protect children online.

Sources indicate that we’re building on our current protections with the release of a newly introduced image classifier that can detect potential CSAM, including AI-generated material. This new classifier looks for visual signs of abuse, helping teams identify novel images that may not have been seen before. It returns scores that help reviewers decide which images may need attention first. This is the first CSAM classifier with broad availability that has a specific signal on indicating if CSAM may be AI generated.

Our teams trained, evaluated, and designed the classifier for real-world deployment with assistance from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC)⁠(opens in a fresh window), a nonprofit that operates the CyberTipline, a centralized reporting hub for the online exploitation of children.

We’re offering access to the classifier to vetted organizations through the OpenAI API at no cost, making CSAM detection more accessible to child safety organizations and the broader industry, including those with teams of varying sizes.

Industry observers note that child safety is an industry-wide issue that requires strong collaboration across organizations and a variety of solutions. We’ve engaged the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a latest window) and ROOST⁠(opens in a new window) to help us share access to this new tool, and we are strong supporters of tools developed by others such as Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window) CSAM detection system. In addition, we recently began participating in the Tech Coalition's Lantern program⁠(opens in a new window), where we will share and receive signals relating to online child sexual exploitation and abuse to strengthen cross- platform collaboration.

It has been revealed that we’ve tested the classifier internally and with early partners to measure how much abusive material it detects, how often it flags other images, and how it can support safety teams. Their feedback helped us identify weaknesses and improve the system.

Early tests suggest the classifier can help reviewers focus on abusive images while reducing review of false positives. In an evaluation of user-uploaded images, we compared the latest classifier with our current protections and found:.

The new classifier could reduce review work: we estimated that it would flag 48% fewer images while finding roughly the same number of abusive images as the existing tool.

Images flagged by the newly introduced classifier were about twice as likely to contain abuse.

Sources indicate that early access partners have also evaluated how the classifier supports their own safety teams. In fal⁠(opens in a new window)’s testing on human-reviewed production images, reviewers confirmed 72% of the classifier’s high-confidence flags as novel CSAM. invideo AI⁠(opens in a new window)’s testing showed one in four flagged cases led to a ban. In SafetyKit⁠(opens in a new window)’s evaluations involving drawings or animations that sexualize children, the classifier detected 90% of cases.

Sources indicate that more information about the classifier is available in the CSAM classifier model card⁠(opens in a newly introduced window). Organizations interested in the classifier will be able to request access through our intake form⁠. We’ll continue improving the classifier with feedback from those that use it.

We already prohibit CSAM, train our models to refuse requests for it, and take action against accounts that violate our policies. We’re building on those safeguards with fresh product warnings in ChatGPT that interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and point people toward help to stop harmful behavior.

The warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated. Alongside the warning, we’ll remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available to help people stop harmful behavior. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.

Recent findings suggest that we developed this approach with input from organizations and academic advisors that research and develop programs to prevent child sexual abuse, including Protect Children⁠(opens in a latest window), the Lucy Faithfull Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), Dr. Caoilte Ó Ciardha, Researcher & Honorary Reader in Forensic Psychology at the University of Kent and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial⁠(opens in a new window) of deterrent messages.

The protection of children online doesn’t end with detection. We’ve published CSAM guidance⁠(opens in a latest window) to give developers practical steps to prevent abuse, detect harmful content, and act on it. Developed with input from the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window), Thorn⁠(opens in a new window), NCMEC⁠(opens in a new window), and the Internet Watch Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), it is designed for organizations at different stages of building their safety systems.

The guidance provides clear rules, ways for owners to report concerns, detection tools, and processes for reviewing and reporting suspected abuse. It also explains how safety identifiers can help developers connect misuse to individual users and how to support the people reviewing sensitive content. Developers can use it alongside tools such as our new image classifier, Moderation API⁠(opens in a new window), ROOST’s self-hosted review console Coop⁠(opens in a new window), and dedicated CSAM detection services such as Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window).

According to recent reports, our commitment to collaboration and supporting the broader developer ecosystem also is reflected in our work with Anthropic and Google to jointly commission new guidance on responding to disclosures of child sexual exploitation and abuse in AI systems. Recently published by the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window), this guidance provides developers with practical recommendations for addressing these sensitive situations.

We’ve already seen this guidance lead to increased numbers of developers accessing child safety tooling and registering to report CSAM to NCMEC.

Sources indicate that protecting children also means supporting the specialist child safety investigators working to find victims and stop abuse. As we’ve discussed publicly with Thorn⁠(opens in a upcoming window), AI can help investigators organize and prioritize information and reduce unnecessary exposure to abusive material.

Sources indicate that we’re also supporting child-safety law enforcement units with upcoming tools and trainings on how to use AI in their investigations, including dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. At launch, the first tool will help investigators review lengthy chat logs and legal process returns, identify potential connections, and create timelines, with findings linked to source material.

The initial training is planned as an overview and demonstration, supported by a practical field guide that teams can refer to afterward. It will introduce the tools and how they fit into investigative work. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. Future iterations of the training will be proposed at regional, national and international conferences.

It has been revealed that these efforts share one goal: preventing harm to children and strengthening the response when abuse occurs. We’ll continue improving our safeguards while empowering child protection organizations, developers, researchers, and investigators with the tools, resources, and expertise they need to protect children, combat exploitation, and bring perpetrators to justice. By working together, we can harness the power of AI to make a meaningful difference in the fight against child sexual exploitation and abuse.

Latest Update: Teaching Students to Stand on Their Own: Distilling Vision Foundation Models for Fine-Grained Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (212 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33749v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fine-grained few-shot class-incremental learning (FG-FSCIL) aims to incrementally learn visually similar newly introduced classes from limited images without catastrophic forgetting. Prior work typically learns strong representations on base classes or leverages vision foundation models (VFMs) directly as backbones or via knowledge distillation. However, VFM backbones incur high computational costs and do not guarantee fine-grained recognition. Although knowledge distillation reduces inference cost, our preliminary experiments reveal that distilled students still lag substantially behind their VFM teachers, particularly on new classes. To address this limitation, we propose STAND, a systematic VFM-to-student distillation design tailored for FG-FSCIL. Specifically, STAND connects the teacher and student by equipping the student with a fixed copy of the teacher's classifier, aligning their outputs via projectors, and feeding both models composite images that combine different training images. On these composite images, relation distillation matches how the teacher and the student relate each image to other images, while difference distillation matches how this relation changes between two composite images. Finally, we freeze the student and classify new classes using length-calibrated prototypes, which restore the reduced similarity of few-shot prototypes. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that STAND achieves state-of-the-art performance across FG-FSCIL datasets at low computational cost, while generalizing across student backbones and broader datasets.

How Spanner Graph detects ads fraud and abuse at Google at multi-billion node scale

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ever wonder how the Google Ads team keeps the massive system stable and online, despite continuous attempts by hackers to take it down?
  • The Google Ads team uses a central graph-based platform to fight fraud and abuse with batch and real-time signals.
  • Industry observers note that the need for a graph-based abuse detection platform stems from how the global threat landscape has evolved.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Director, Engineering, Google Ads.

Group Product Manager, Data Cloud.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Ever wonder how the Google Ads team keeps the massive system stable and online, despite continuous attempts by hackers to take it down? Part of the answer is using Spanner as its core operational and graph database.

The Google Ads team uses a central graph-based platform to fight fraud and abuse with batch and real-time signals. Built to protect the Google Ads ecosystem and now used by multiple teams across Google, the platform organizes anti-abuse intelligence into a single, interconnected view. Its core mission is simple but critical: uncover hidden connections between malicious assets in real time before they can harm people or advertisers. This blog talks about the challenging modern fraud and abuse landscape, and how Spanner, specifically Spanner Graph, helps Google successfully detect those threats.

Industry observers note that the need for a graph-based abuse detection platform stems from how the global threat landscape has evolved. Digital advertising fraud and online scams are no longer minor operational nuisances, they are a massive drain on the global economy. According to the NASDAQ Global Financial Crime Report, total global fraud losses are estimated at nearly $580 billion for 2025. Furthermore, global surveys indicate that approximately one in five adults fall victim to scams. In digital ads, fraud and abuse waste marketing spend, corrupt attribution data, and expose everyday customers to financial scams, identity theft, and malware.

Bad actors are increasingly leveraging automation and AI to scale deceptive campaigns more efficiently. In 2025 alone, Google blocked or removed more than 8.3 billion policy-violating ads and suspended 24.9 million advertiser accounts. As these tactics evolve, real-time detection becomes more key for protecting businesses and users.

Defending applications from fraud and abuse requires continuously advancing threat detection beyond traditional, point-in-time checks. To do that, modern security systems must address two compounding challenges simultaneously:.

Industry observers note that fraud and abuse operate as networks: Bad actors hide behind residential proxies and synthetic identities to create deceptive ad campaigns. Each of the attributes like location proxies, account, and identity parameters  appear benign in isolation. But behind the scenes, bad actors share payment methods, domains, and accounts, requiring security systems to target entire coordinated clusters of fraud rather than isolated indicators. This is hard to capture with traditional approaches that do not understand the relationship between attributes and evaluates each signal separately.

Detection must scale dynamically: As the graph-based abuse detection platform grew, the previous system, based on offline MapReduce batch processing, became bottlenecked. Tracing multi-hop relationships in batch MapReduce required repeated, expensive joins across distributed stages, triggering massive intermediate data expansions, heavy shuffle overhead, and network bottlenecks that caused hours-long latencies and combinatorial fanouts during multi-hop traversals.

According to recent reports, in critical scenarios like halting live malware campaigns, multi-hour latency gaps leave room for a lot of damage. To block sophisticated fraud rings, Google needed to evaluate multi-hop relationship risks in real time at the time of serving these ads, before malicious content reaches users.

To overcome the limits of processing at inference time, the engineering team needed a database that could ingest live signals from a large number of sources via pub/sub streams, all while delivering horizontal elasticity, global transactional consistency, and sub-second multi-hop traversals. The solution was to modernize Google's graph-based abuse detection platform for Ads onto Spanner Graph.

Industry observers note that because Ads’ core transactional and entity data already lived in Spanner, they didn’t need to migrate any data in order to adopt Spanner Graph. Rather than standing up a separate, specialized graph database, the team simply defined property graphs directly on top of their existing relational tables.

This delivered several benefits:.

From hour-long batch jobs to sub-second queries: Spanner Graph co-locates graph traversal computations directly with the underlying distributed data splits to minimize join overhead. Multi-hop traversals that previously took an hour in offline Apache Flume MapReduce jobs now execute on live production data with sub-second to single-digit millisecond latency.

According to recent reports, zero-ETL adoption in weeks, not months: Because there was no data to move, most graph-based abuse detection use cases transitioned to Spanner Graph within weeks. Layering a graph directly onto existing Spanner tables eliminated fragile synchronization pipelines and redundant storage costs.

Expressive pattern matching with native ISO GQL: Instead of writing and maintaining complex custom traversal code, engineers now query the exact same tables using standard ISO Graph Query Language (GQL), significantly accelerating feature velocity.

With Spanner Graph, Google's graph-based abuse detection platform for ads performs multi-hop pattern matching directly against operational relational data using ISO GQL. For instance, when an account is flagged for suspicious activity, the platform does real-time traversals to uncover all connected signals across the graph. This allows security systems to identify and disable entire coordinated fraud rings rapidly rather than handling individual accounts sequentially.

It has been revealed that here’s how it works. The following query uses full-text keyword search and vector similarity search to traverse connected entities across multiple hops to identify a target entity linked to known suspicious activity. Five-model Blackwell calibration gives zero false rejections across 1.85M GEMM/MoE blocks and 1.96M non-GEMM rows. Our zero-Phase-2 folded backend (folded ZK simulator open) proves Qwen3-0.6B ExtSeed-153 (1.47B cells, 8 MiB) in 450.2 s GPU (10.76 s CPU) at unique-decoding $Q=128$, passes a 14/14 cheating matrix, and scales to 36-layer Qwen3-4B (dev $4+2$) and live vLLM Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 Relation 6 (1.49 s prove, 23.4 ms Rust verify, public weight tiles). arXiv:2611.33722v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: People become faster at a task through practice, but models that improve with experience do not necessarily learn to use less computation. We train looped models, whose intermediate predictions allow earlier exits, to perform tasks with fewer iterations through practice. This is difficult because shared-weight updates can degrade the final-loop prediction while improving early ones, and the exit gate must track early predictions as their quality changes. We propose FLUENT, which requires no additional task labels or rewards: it distills the initial model's final-loop prediction into early predictions, anchors the current final-loop prediction to the same frozen teacher, and trains the exit gate to balance disagreement with the current final-loop prediction against computation cost. FLUENT improves performance at shallower depth in upcoming Crafter worlds, raises LIBERO success with fewer action-head iterations, and maintains language-model accuracy at lower selected depth. On a real robot, success rises from 62.3\% to 74.6\% while mean time over successful episodes falls from 69\,s to 31\,s. The project page is available at https://msseok96-cpu.github.io/FLUENT/.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.33700v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conversational sports analytics requires accurate, evidence-based responses with low latency. Changes in query distributions, data resources, and model behavior can degrade static agent configurations, motivating controlled evolution guided by runtime evidence. We present Sports Agent, a self-evolving framework integrating an Agentic SQL Model for structured-data reasoning, a harness for planning and tool orchestration, and a unified Feedback Engine connecting online execution with offline evolution. The engine assesses responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, diagnoses failures, and generates evolution signals. Model evolution combines SQL-to-Question Scaling for coverage expansion with Graph-Guided Scaling for error-targeted synthesis. Generated questions undergo trajectory distillation and quality filtering for iterative supervised fine-tuning, followed by a separate Post-RL stage. Harness evolution translates recurrent failures into bounded prompt and skill updates, validated through independent audits, execution replay, and regression testing. Performance-tolerance checks guard against unacceptable degradation during simplification. The resulting Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-based model outperforms Qwen3.8-Max on sports question answering and analysis while achieving approximately three times the inference efficiency. Across 30 harness-evolution rounds, the aggregate performance score improves by 10.8 points. In a live sports analytics product, the evolved system improves factual correctness by 10.5 points and average response length, a proxy for answer richness, by 158.1%, while reducing average latency by 41.3% relative to the baseline.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 16, 2026 · Research · Science.

We’re expanding the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to give up to 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to ChatGPT.

Industry observers note that the program began as a pilot in July. Applications for the next round open Monday, November 23. We’ll award 50,000 newly introduced grants to eligible researchers on a first-come, first-served basis. Each grant gives the recipient and up to two collaborators free access to ChatGPT Plus. If you’re already on the waitlist and qualify, we’ll email you before applications open with instructions for activating your account.

In a recent development, participants can use OpenAI’s frontier models and get training on how to use ChatGPT in their research. By default, we don’t use data shared through the program to train our models.

Waitlist signups by country or territory as of November 12, 2026. Darker colors indicate more signups on a logarithmic scale.

According to recent reports, 20,000 researchers in 33 countries have joined the program since the pilot began in July. Shuqi Li, a researcher at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, looks for upcoming drug targets that could ultimately shorten tuberculosis treatment. He is exploring whether ChatGPT can help link lab and patient data to speed up antibiotic development. Arthur Porto, assistant curator of AI biodiversity at the Florida Museum of Natural History, and his team uses AI tools to turn photographs of museum specimens into searchable databases. They also created a 3D model of a butterfly whose wings change color as you turn it, just like the real specimen.

We’re also publishing Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT, new research from our Economic Research team examining how more than 1,800 researchers used ChatGPT during the program’s summer pilot. Surveyed participants estimated that, without AI, the same research work at the same quality would have taken nearly twice as long.

According to recent reports, we want more researchers to have the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions and make discoveries that improve people’s lives. That is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

According to recent reports, the program’s summer pilot helped us understand how researchers use ChatGPT and how we can improve their experience. Based on feedback from researchers, we’re moving away from lottery-based selection. For the next round, we’ll provide access to the first 50,000 applications who meet the eligibility requirements.

The pilot gave researchers access to ChatGPT Pro. When we reviewed pilot usage, we found that most participants would have stayed within ChatGPT Plus usage limits. Based on that finding, we’re offering Plus for newly introduced grants so we can extend access to more research teams.

Each grant for this round covers the recipient and up to two collaborators, supporting up to 150,000 researchers. Our goal for the program as a whole is to reach 200,000 researchers, double the goal we declared when the pilot launched in July.

It has been revealed that we’ll continue learning from participants about the application process, the capabilities they need, and the support that helps them use these tools in their research. This feedback will help us refine the program and shape future rounds.

Recent findings suggest that different scientific fields will use AI in different ways, and researchers will need different kinds and levels of support. We’re working with scientific communities to understand those needs and shape our tools, training, and programs around them.

According to recent reports, our support also includes helping scientific communities turn AI-generated results into deeper understanding and newly introduced discoveries. In mathematics, we contributed $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative⁠ to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI.

Recent findings suggest that we’re also providing different ways for researchers and institutions to access our tools. ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is just one way we’re helping researchers access advanced AI tools.

Through ChatGPT Edu⁠(opens in a new window), universities can give their campus communities access to ChatGPT for research, teaching, and learning, with tools for analyzing data and administrative controls for managing access.

Industry observers note that for researchers working in biology, GPT‑Rosalind⁠ brings together specialized biological reasoning and access to scientific tools and databases. The Rosalind Academic Blueprint⁠ helps bring these capabilities to eligible labs at U.S. universities, offering up to 30 seats at no cost for up to 12 months. Access to GPT‑Rosalind requires approval through our trusted-access process.

Visit our researcher access guide to learn more about ChatGPT Edu, GPT‑Rosalind, and ChatGPT for Academic Researchers.

Industry observers note that as these efforts grow, researchers’ experiences will help us understand where our tools are useful, where they fall short, and what support is needed. We’ll use that feedback to improve our programs, develop training and learning resources, and create opportunities for researchers to exchange approaches with one another.

Our goal is to give more researchers the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions—and to keep improving that support as their research and our capabilities evolve.

Learn more about the program⁠(opens in a newly introduced window).

Breaking: Rethinking Sequential Locate-Then-Edit: Optimality and Stability

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (188 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33692v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Locate-Then-Edit framework enables efficient knowledge updates in large language models without requiring full retraining. Recent research has increasingly focused on sequential editing, where knowledge arrives continuously and the model is updated incrementally. However, existing sequential methods commonly suffer from catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only a few hundred edits. In contrast, batch editing - which jointly optimizes all edits and yields the optimal solution under a specified editing objective - can support tens of thousands of edits with high edit efficacy while preserving the model's general capabilities, resulting in a substantial performance gap between the two editing paradigms. In this paper, we demonstrate that this gap can be closed via a batch-equivalent sequential editing approach. Moreover, we investigate the underlying mechanism of model degradation in existing sequential methods by analyzing the convergence behavior of weight perturbations as edits accumulate. Our analysis reveals that current methods typically exhibit linear or logarithmic growth in perturbation, whereas the proposed batch-equivalent method achieves time-invariant growth, thereby theoretically guaranteeing long-term stability and preserving the integrity of pretrained knowledge throughout massive-scale sequential editing.

arXiv:2611.33687v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal memory enables long-horizon vision-language agents to preserve and retrieve past experiences. While prior research has focused on memory construction and retrieval, effectively using the provided memory remains a challenge for vision-language models (VLMs). We find that VLMs often fail to answer downstream questions even when sufficient multimodal evidence is provided. To investigate why VLMs struggle, we replace memory images with reference captions and observe substantial performance gains, suggesting difficulties in reading visual evidence directly. However, model-generated captions may omit critical information, limiting this approach in practice. These limitations motivate a closer examination of memory utilization, revealing failures in both evidence reading and downstream question answering. Building on this distinction, we propose \textbf{MemRU}, a two-stage training framework that improves evidence reading through supervised fine-tuning (Read SFT) and downstream evidence utilization through Group Relative Policy Optimization (Use GRPO). Experimental results demonstrate that our 8B model generalizes across three unseen multimodal memory systems, outperforming Qwen3-VL-32B and approaching GPT-5-mini.

What Is Redundant at High Resolution? Efficient Attention and Feed-Forward Design for All-in-One Image Restoration

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (204 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.33636v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-scale architectures are widely adopted in all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) to capture larger-scale context at low-resolution stages and refine details at high-resolution (HR) stages. However, processing spatially large feature maps at HR stages incurs substantial computational costs and memory traffic, making efficient HR processing challenging. To address this challenge, we propose High-resolution Global-Local Restoration (HiGLR), an efficient multi-scale AIO-IR network grounded in an analysis of spatial redundancy in self-attention and convolutional feed-forward networks (ConvFFNs). Specifically, this analysis identifies three key redundancies: per-query readout at the finest-scale stage, key routing across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and spatial mixing in the expanded feature spaces of ConvFFNs. Accordingly, HiGLR replaces costly self-attention at the finest-scale stage with a learned input-independent kernel. At intermediate stages, we propose a Block-Routed Hybrid Attention, which combines coarse-scale dense attention with fine-scale block-sparse attention over value residuals relative to coarse summaries, and shares routing indices across neighboring queries. We further introduce a Dual-Space FFN that performs spatial mixing in a compact space and pointwise nonlinear transformation in an expanded space, enabling efficient kernel fusion. Combining these designs, HiGLR achieves state-of-the-art performance while delivering up to a $4.24\times$ inference speedup over existing methods.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, our latest model configuration earned leading marks on multiple benchmarks. Every ChatGPT Enterprise customer can now request access.

In a recent development, today, we're releasing an updated Astra for Law that is state-of-the-art on Harvey LAB-AA and a top performer on Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench. We are also enabling all ChatGPT Enterprise customers to request access through the Trusted Access Program, including through the API.

In a recent development, astra for Law is a model configuration of GPT‑6.2 Astra⁠, our latest, most powerful frontier model. It pairs GPT‑6.2 Astra with an expanded legal search index and instructions for researching a question, weighing the authorities, and writing the answer. Today’s configuration earned full credit on the LAB-AA tests nearly 40% more often than did the runner-up, GPT‑6.2 Astra.

Since we introduced Astra for Law in September⁠ to a small group of firms, including Cooley⁠, Ropes & Gray⁠, and Sullivan & Cromwell⁠, our research team has made rapid innovations to improve its legal reasoning and expand its legal search index by over a third. On Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench⁠(opens in a latest window), the share of research answers that passed every check rose from about 46% to 53.8% in less than two months.

As the world grows more complex, lawyers occupy an increasingly important role. They shape nearly every system we rely on: they negotiate the agreements that move commerce, defend people’s rights in courts, and draft the laws we all live by. That’s why we’ve made law a research priority at OpenAI: to put the best intelligence in the hands of the best lawyers.

Sources indicate that harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) tests whether a model can take a legal assignment from start to finish. LAB-AA⁠(opens in a fresh window) is Artificial Analysis’s version of that test. It tests the models on 120 assignments developed by Harvey across 24 areas of law – everything from drafting deposition outlines to reviewing commercial leases to strategizing ownership changes in acquisitions. To earn full credit, an answer must meet every requirement of an assignment without hallucinating, i.e., making a material claim that is not supported by the source documents.

Astra for Law ranked first, earning full credit on 20.8% of assignments, ahead of GPT‑6.2 Astra at 15.0% and Muse Wonder Full at 13.1%.

Astra for Law ranked first at 20.8%, earning full credit about 59% more often than Muse Wonder Full, the highest-scoring non-OpenAI model.

An asterisk indicates no publicly available API.

Astra for Law also earned that top score with 54% less output per assignment than the highest-scoring non-OpenAI model in the evaluation, averaging about 64,000 output tokens per assignment, compared with 139,000 for Muse Wonder Full. For legal teams paying by usage, this can mean the difference between staying within budget and blowing through it.

In a recent development, each dot is a model configuration. Higher means more assignments earned full credit; farther left means fewer output tokens, which include the text a model generates as it reasons and writes. Astra for Law averaged about 64,000 output tokens per assignment and earned full credit on 20.8%, compared with 139,000 and 13.1% for Muse Wonder Full. No configuration shown matched Astra for Law’s score using fewer output tokens.

Sources indicate that the dotted line shows the Pareto frontier. Token counts are rounded to the nearest thousand.

According to recent reports, hallucinations are unacceptable in legal work. A single invented citation can cost a lawyer a client’s trust, credibility in court, and a reputation built over years. That’s why reducing hallucinations has been a priority for Astra for Law. In Artificial Analysis’s latest LAB-AA comparison, Astra for Law tied (with GPT‑6) for the lowest rate of material hallucinations: 0.03 per assignment, compared with 0.59 for Claude Opus 5.5 (the next lowest non-OpenAI model). Notably, Astra for Law's performance on this eval included zero material hallucinations for tasks that met the all-pass criteria.

Astra for Law averaged 0.03 material and 0.06 minor hallucinations per assignment. Claude Opus 5.5 averaged 0.59 material and 0.51 minor hallucinations per assignment, about 20 times as many material hallucinations and 8.5 times as many minor ones.

Material errors can mislead readers on substantive points; minor errors are unlikely to affect legal interpretation. Only material errors affect the headline score. Grid-patterned bars indicate no publicly available API.

We've made law a research priority at OpenAI, dedicating a team of researchers to accelerate innovation for frontier legal intelligence. One early measure of their progress comes from Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench⁠(opens in a new window), where practicing lawyers set questions about U.S. federal and state law. An answer has to cover every required point and pass the source checks. In September, Astra for Law earned full credit on about 46% of questions. In Vals AI’s November 16 evaluation, it earned full credit on 112 of 208 questions (53.8%), a gain of about eight percentage points in under two months. Across all questions, it earned 90.9% of the available points, including partial credit.

Building Astra for Law as a model configuration lets us stay on the bleeding edge of the frontier, in this case GPT‑6.2 Astra⁠. Industry News: The Detour Is the Danger: Preserving Security During LLM Agent Recovery

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (184 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.33605v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external tools and reusable Skills to execute complex workflows, autonomously replanning when operations fail. However, such recovery may preserve task functionality while silently discarding the security protections required by the original workflow. In this paper, we investigate workflow security downgrade, a failure-induced security threat in which agents execute sensitive operations without satisfying their original protection requirements. Unlike prompt injection, this threat exploits autonomous recovery decisions triggered by execution failures, without modifying instructions or tool definitions. We systematically evaluate this behavior through fault injection in an executable MCP/Skill environment spanning seven LLMs, twelve task templates, and three security-sensitive domains. To address this threat, we propose ARGUS, an obligation-preserving recovery framework that combines resource-bound security evidence, isolated recovery-plan validation, and execution-time enforcement. In a separate 864-run evaluation, ARGUS prevents all observed protection-loss events under enforcement, while recovery assistance yields model-dependent improvements in protected task completion over blocking alone. Our findings demonstrate that secure agent recovery requires preserving security obligations across workflow changes, rather than merely restoring task functionality.

DexEngine first places each clip's hand-object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand-object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

RankCast: Phase-Aware Rank Balancing in MoE Serving

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (270 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.33542v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern large language model (LLM) inference increasingly adopts disaggregated architectures that separate Prefill (P) and Decode (D) phases. Meanwhile, Expert Parallelism (EP) has been widely adopted in large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model serving. However, load imbalance still slows down MoE inference because each layer must wait for the busiest EP rank. The main source of latency differs between prefill and decode. Prefill is compute-bound, and its MoE layers' latency is determined by the maximum token count of the busiest rank. At the same time, under moderate batch sizes, Decode is memory-bound, so the latency is dominated by the maximum active-expert count across ranks. To solve both problems under a unified framework, we present RankCast, a system that reduces rank-level maximum token counts during prefill and active-expert counts during decode. For every token, RankCast preserves the predicted Top-p experts and chooses the remaining k-p from its Top-L candidates (L > k). In prefill, RankCast yields a price per rank that steers flexible assignments to less loaded ranks. In decode, RankCast closes experts on the busiest ranks while preserving the constraints for each token. Both paths are implemented and tested in the state-of-the-art inference frameworks SGLang and DeepEP. We overlap RankCast's kernels with model execution and reuse the existing DeepEP communication channel for metadata transmission. On Qwen3-235B-A22B with EP=8 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with EP=16, RankCast removes over 75% of the busiest rank's excess prefill load, improves prefill input throughput by up to 19%, and reduces decode time per output token by up to 10%. The quality cost is below one percentage point.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we’re launching OpenAI for Chile, a partnership with the Government of Chile, led by the Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation, to support responsible AI adoption in public administration, build civil servants’ skills and help local startups develop useful AI applications.

The partnership builds on Chile’s National AI Policy and action plan⁠(opens in a latest window), which support talent development, research and responsible adoption.

The Memorandum of Understanding was signed on the sidelines of Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference in California, with Minister Ximena Lincolao leading the agreement on behalf of Chile.

It has been revealed that the partnership is supported by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s American SI Exports Program⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), of which OpenAI is an anchor partner, helping Chile advance its own AI ambitions through public sector innovation, skills development, and entrepreneurship.

The partnership will explore technology adoption in the ministry’s administrative processes, including potential support from OpenAI on adopting new models, alongside advice and training for ministry personnel.

For civil servants, the partnership will explore practical AI literacy, upskilling and reskilling tailored to their roles. Activities could include workshops and a train-the-trainer approach, covering effective use of AI tools, checking outputs, protecting sensitive information and maintaining human oversight.

In a recent development, to support Chile’s AI startup and innovation ecosystem, the partners will explore access to relevant OpenAI programs and technology, practical learning, technical guidance and mentorship. Cooperation could also connect entrepreneurs with public institutions, universities and other local partners to develop applications that support Chile’s economic development and public-service priorities.

A joint task force of ministry and OpenAI representatives is expected to agree priorities and an initial workplan, with leads, milestones and measures of success for each activity.

It has been revealed that specific activities, eligibility, resources and access to technology will be agreed separately. The MoU sets no investment or purchasing commitment. Activities will be subject to appropriate safeguards for privacy, information security and responsible use.

According to recent reports, openAI for Chile is part of OpenAI for Countries, our global initiative to help countries use AI to advance their national priorities, strengthen their economies and expand opportunity. We work with governments and local partners to turn AI’s potential into practical benefits for their people.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: PRECEPT: Security Self-Improvement of Coding Agents via Evolving Principles

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (293 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33519v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI coding agents increasingly write and submit code with limited human review, and much of it passes functional tests while remaining insecure. We show that these failures persist. Across 14 task sequences, Codex, Claude Code, and Qwen Code fixed a vulnerability 85.7% of the time when shown the failing security test, then reintroduced the same vulnerability class in a fresh session 26.7% of the time, about as often as agents that had never seen it (27.5%). The capability is present; the retention is not. Neither recording the repair in the agent's persistent context nor supplying published secure coding principles closed the gap: the recorded fix stayed tied to the family of the task it came from, and the principles, written for human developers, remained too general to apply to the code at hand. The knowledge exists; it is not activated. We call the missing ability security self-improvement: an agent learns from its own security failures so that each lesson persists across sessions, applies to new code, and does not break what works. We present PRECEPT, which equips coding agents with this ability through an evolving library that starts from authoritative secure coding principles and revises them against the agent's own failures, so that each principle comes to fire on the code where that agent actually goes wrong. A revision is kept only if fresh executions show it makes code more secure while keeping functional success within a small tolerance of the agent without the library. Improvement continues across evolution steps rather than saturating after the first. On task families never seen during evolution, PRECEPT's weakest agent reaches 97.1% secure working code, above the strongest unaided agent at 81.9% and the strongest baseline at 87.7%.
