BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?

📅 01 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1407 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 📄 Tech Report: http://allenai.org/papers/benchmirt | 📊 Data: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/benchmirt | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/BenchMIRT.
  • Today we’re introducing BenchMIRT, a newly introduced method for auditing LLM benchmarks at the level of individual prompts—the questions and tasks a model is scored on.
  • A benchmark is usually designed to measure a particular ability, such as safety, general reasoning, or instruction following.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Tech Report: http://allenai.org/papers/benchmirt | 📊 Data: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/benchmirt | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/BenchMIRT.

Today we’re introducing BenchMIRT, a newly introduced method for auditing LLM benchmarks at the level of individual prompts—the questions and tasks a model is scored on.

A benchmark is usually designed to measure a particular ability, such as safety, general reasoning, or instruction following. But the individual tasks inside it may depend on more than that stated goal. Take BBQ, a benchmark designed to test whether models rely on social stereotypes. One question asks about a grandson and grandfather trying to book an Uber. It probes age bias, but also requires the model to track who’s who and reason from the evidence provided rather than assumptions.

And even within a single benchmark, different groups of questions and tasks can measure different things. WildJailbreak, for example, includes harmful jailbreak prompts alongside benign prompts designed to test whether a model refuses harmless requests too often. The harmful prompts are more closely associated with safety, while the benign prompts are more closely associated with general reasoning. Averaging them into a single benchmark score can obscure that difference.

According to recent reports, benchMIRT helps researchers separate those signals and see what’s actually driving a benchmark’s score. It does this by analyzing how models perform on each question or task and estimating which underlying capabilities are most closely associated with getting it right.

BenchMIRT takes cues from Item Response Theory (IRT), a technique originating in psychometrics—the field concerned with measuring abilities and traits from patterns of test responses. IRT starts from a simple idea: not every question tells you the same amount about the person taking a test. Some are harder than others, and some do a better job of distinguishing stronger performers from weaker ones.

In a recent development, researchers have previously applied single-dimensional IRT to individual benchmarks, including in our Fluid Benchmarking work. BenchMIRT extends that approach with multidimensional IRT, or MIRT, allowing it to separate multiple capabilities that may contribute to performance on the same questions.

BenchMIRT applies IRT at both the model and question level. For a given model, it estimates the model’s strength on the capabilities reflected across the selected benchmarks. For each question, it estimates how difficult the question is and how well it distinguishes models that are stronger or weaker on those capabilities.

We trained BenchMIRT on benchmarking results from 100 LLMs across 16 benchmarks and more than 34K questions. Six of those benchmarks measure general reasoning, including MMLU-Pro, GPQA, MATH, and BBH. The other 10 come from our Olmo 3 safety suite, including HarmBench, StrongReject, WildJailbreak, BBQ, WMDP, and XSTest.

It has been revealed that crucially, we didn’t tell BenchMIRT which benchmarks were measuring which capabilities. It independently recovered two dominant dimensions: safety and general reasoning. When we repeated our analysis from scratch, those same two dimensions emerged each time, suggesting the result was stable rather than specific to one analysis.

For many benchmarks, BenchMIRT largely confirmed their intended focus: strong performance on reasoning benchmarks tracked with reasoning ability, while strong performance on jailbreak and harmful-content benchmarks tracked with safety.

But BenchMIRT also revealed a more complicated picture in some evaluations.

According to recent reports, BBQ, which evaluates social bias and is commonly grouped with safety benchmarks, aligned much more strongly with general reasoning in BenchMIRT’s analysis. That means a low BBQ score may partly reflect difficulty understanding or reasoning through certain questions, rather than safety behavior alone.

According to recent reports, WMDP behaves differently from most safety benchmarks. It tests dangerous dual-use knowledge in areas such as biology, chemistry, and cybersecurity—for example, knowledge that could help someone misuse a biological agent or exploit a computer system. BenchMIRT found that WMDP scores were more strongly associated with general reasoning than with safety. Stronger general reasoning, however, was associated with lower WMDP scores, because the benchmark counts refusing or failing to provide the dangerous knowledge as the desired response.

Industry observers note that these findings don’t necessarily mean the benchmarks are flawed or incomplete. Rather, they show that a single benchmark score can combine several different signals—and that BenchMIRT can help disentangle those signals and make the score easier to interpret.

Item difficulty and discrimination in both dimensions for Harmbench. Dimension 0 models the safety dimension, while Dimension 1 maps to the general reasoning dimension.

Bar size and direction show the Pearson correlation, across 100 open-weight LLMs, between BenchMIRT ability scores and benchmark scores on a −1 to 1 scale—pink for general reasoning and teal for safety; bars extending left of center are negative. Bold with underline marks each row’s stronger correlation, except where the two are too close to separate; asterisks mark p < 0.01.

BenchMIRT can also help identify which questions in an evaluation are most informative about the capability the benchmark is trying to measure.

Using BenchMIRT’s question-level estimates, we ranked questions across the same 16 benchmarks used to train BenchMIRT and kept those that did the best job of distinguishing stronger from weaker models, while still preserving a mix of easier and harder questions.

Across those benchmarks, keeping only 10% of the questions generally preserved nearly the same picture of which models were stronger or weaker on the underlying safety or reasoning capability as using the full set. Keeping 50% of the questions often matched the full benchmark’s measure of those capabilities even more closely.

Industry observers note that benchMIRT can also use the patterns it learns across models and questions to predict how a model would perform on a benchmark question it hasn’t been observed answering. In our experiments, it correctly predicted whether a model would answer a held-out question correctly 79% of the time. By comparison, a simpler approach that assumes a model will perform on each question about as well as it does on the benchmark overall was correct 70% of the time.

In practice, that means BenchMIRT can estimate model performance more precisely from what it has already learned about the model’s abilities and the demands of each question, without needing to evaluate every model on every question.

It has been revealed that benchMIRT offers a way to better understand and refine the benchmarks researchers use to evaluate model capabilities. By looking at individual questions rather than only overall scores, it can reveal when a benchmark mixes together different capabilities, identify clusters of questions that behave differently from the rest, and surface questions that add little useful information about the capability the benchmark is meant to measure.

Sources indicate that there are important limitations. The models we used to train and evaluate BenchMIRT were all released by March 2025, so our analysis doesn’t capture how BenchMIRT behaves on newer generations of LLMs. And the dimensions BenchMIRT discovers depend on the benchmark set it’s given—safety and reasoning emerged as the dominant dimensions across the 16 benchmarks we selected for this project, but a different mix of evaluations could surface different underlying capabilities.

Sources indicate that there are trade-offs, too. If the goal is to rank models by their predicted performance on randomly held-out items, the benchmark’s average score performs slightly better than BenchMIRT. BenchMIRT’s advantage is the finer-grained picture it provides of performance on individual questions.

Industry observers note that that question-level detail can also cut both ways: the same estimates that help identify a benchmark’s most informative safety questions could be used to remove them, producing a weaker evaluation that an unsafe model could pass. Existing tools already make it possible to trim evaluations in similar ways, and we think the added transparency into what benchmark questions are actually measuring is worth that risk—but it’s a real one.

Still, we see BenchMIRT – and future tools like it – as a step toward more targeted benchmark design and efficient evaluation. By showing which questions are actually driving a benchmark’s results, these approaches could help researchers build evaluations that are smaller, more focused, and easier to interpret, while giving a clearer picture of the capabilities they’re meant to measure.

Good read! Reliable evaluation is essential for understanding how well AI systems perform and where they need improvement. Benchmarking and systematic testing can help developers make better decisions about model selection, application quality, and readiness for real-world use. In Generative AI app development, these practices are particularly useful for identifying limitations before expanding access or introducing additional features. Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.33254v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Online discussion of generative AI has become increasingly contentious, and communities devoted to supporting, opposing, or debating AI have emerged on social media. Some of these communities take anti-AI actions, such as deploying crawler tarpits and data-poisoning services to interfere with data collection and model training. Yet, the scope of these actions and their relationship to online discourse remain poorly understood. In this paper, we present the first measurement study of online conflict over generative AI, from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions. We collect 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities, label them with a large language model detector validated against human labels, identify 3,312 anti-AI actions, and trace the output of three deployed anti-AI tools. Our analysis reveals that 30.0% of posts in communities devoted to this conflict are toxic, compared to 4.4% in general AI communities. Anti-AI actions in these communities mainly target AI crawling or model training data, such as image cloaking and data poisoning. We further examine the implications of these anti-AI actions for AI training, by analyzing the text and code generated from deployed tools. Notably, 66.5% of the code samples generated by a data-poisoning service contain fabricated facts, misused APIs, or broken logic, yet 93.6% passes a public code-curation pipeline, close to the rate for real source code (95.0%). For crawler tarpit output, adding a period to the end of each paragraph increases the curation survival rate from 16.4% to 91.9%. We also find that crawler tarpit and data-poisoning output has already entered Common Crawl, a widely used public web archive, and that crawler tarpit output has also entered FineWeb, a released pretraining dataset. We hope our study can facilitate a better understanding of online conflict over generative AI and its implications for content moderation and AI training.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In global maritime logistics, Marine Ports and Terminals play a significant role in the movement of container and cargo, within and beyond.
  • It has been revealed that developed by Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), DynaPORT is a field-proven next-generation Terminal Operating System that provides a single, integrated operating backbone for multimodal and multipurpose terminals.
  • It has been revealed that one of India’s largest commercial port developers and operators has relied on DynaPORT for more than two decades across its cargo terminals, supporting the management of bulk, break-bulk, and liquid cargo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

In global maritime logistics, Marine Ports and Terminals play a significant role in the movement of container and cargo, within and beyond. Marine ports and terminals world-wide use a Terminal Operating System (TOS) which acts as the central nervous system managing port operations 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. A modern TOS prepares, automates and orchestrates every physical and digital activities, resources and events across Order-to-Invoice processes of a marine terminal.

It has been revealed that developed by Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), DynaPORT is a field-proven next-generation Terminal Operating System that provides a single, integrated operating backbone for multimodal and multipurpose terminals. It orchestrates the complete order-to-invoice lifecycle across vessel, rail, truck, and barge operations, while supporting containers, general cargo, dry and liquid bulk, break-bulk, and roll-on/roll-off cargo. By automating end-to-end terminal workflows, DynaPORT delivers real-time operational visibility into operations while optimizing assets and resources to drive improvement of key business performance indicators.

It has been revealed that one of India’s largest commercial port developers and operators has relied on DynaPORT for more than two decades across its cargo terminals, supporting the management of bulk, break-bulk, and liquid cargo. To modernize the platform’s architecture, TCS partnered with the customer to achieve a landmark milestone: migrating DynaPORT to a modern, cloud-based architecture.

Industry observers note that the Port Operator & TCS partnered with Google Cloud to execute an ambitious cloud modernization journey. Modeled after the architectural principles of high-velocity Google Cloud enterprise transformations—this case study details the systematic deconstruction of legacy technical debt, the strategic rationale and enterprise differentiators of choosing AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, the target Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and AlloyDB cloud-native architecture, the heterogeneous migration of over 1.2 million lines of code using Google Cloud Database Migration Service (DMS).

Enterprise logistics platforms that evolve over decades inevitably accumulate architectural debt, particularly through tightly coupled components. DynaPORT Cargo followed this pattern: successive releases and architectural transitions gradually transformed the platform into a classic multi-tier monolith, with its components carrying significant technical debt.

Over years of optimization for sub-millisecond on-premises database round-trips, fundamental business logic had been progressively migrated out of the application tier and embedded directly into the database engine. In the DynaPORT Cargo module alone, the core schema contained:.

262 Packages containing over 1.2 million lines of code.

54 Stored Procedures, 53 Functions, and 63 Database Triggers.

Cross-schema User-Defined Types (UDTs).

Critical business operations—such as multi-tiered marine invoice tariff calculations, dynamic slab rating, berth allocation planning, yard truck assignments, and autonomous error logging—were entirely governed by complex, multi-thousand-line PL/SQL procedures. The database was no longer merely a relational persistence store; it was the primary execution engine of the enterprise.

Sources indicate that the application tier was hosted on monolithic WebLogic and WildFly application servers running on static on-premises virtual machines. The application relied on legacy Java Enterprise features, including Enterprise JavaBeans (EJBs), custom Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) dialects, and heavy configuration state. Modules including Revenue Management, Berth Planning, Gate Operations, and Reporting shared common JVM heaps across application servers. A performance spike in batch invoice generation could starve memory from real-time Handheld Terminals (HHT) used by container crane operators on the quayside.

Because business logic was fragmented across Java application binaries and raw database packages, continuous delivery was practically non-existent:.

Manual Deployment Runbooks: Releases required multi-hour maintenance windows involving manual execution of sequential SQL scripts, package recompilations, and server restarts.

High Regression Risk: In the legacy schema with 262 interdependent packages, modifying a single package specification frequently invalidated dozens of dependent functions, views, and synonyms, triggering cascading runtime failures.

Environment Drift: Development, testing, and production environments suffered from configuration divergence, requiring lengthy manual reconciliation before any production cutover.

Licensing fees scaled linearly with physical CPU core counts, penalizing the business whenever hardware was scaled to accommodate peak cargo vessel traffic. Furthermore, high-availability setups required complex shared storage arrays, specialized interconnects, and heavy administrative overhead from dedicated database administrators (DBAs).

When architecting the cloud transformation, the joint architecture teams from the customer, TCS, and Google Cloud evaluated two fundamentally different modernization strategies:.

Strategy A: Database-Agnostic Migration.

Strategy B: Modernization using AlloyDB.

Extract all business logic from the database tier and rewrite it into Java application-tier services (HQL / Spring Data).

Retain optimized procedural logic in the database tier, converting to PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL on AlloyDB.

It has been revealed that massive. Complete rewrite of thousands of data access objects, ORM mappings, and transaction boundaries.

In a recent development, moderate. Focused remediation of syntax, metadata, and database dialect differences; application remains stable.

Multiple person-years; prohibitive time-to-market.

Target delivery achievable in agile sprints; low operational disruption.

Network latency amplification due to multiple network hops for complex set operations previously run in-database.

Native in-engine execution with sub-millisecond response times, backed by AlloyDB’s accelerated storage and compute engine.

Rejected due to timeline risks and massive business disruption.

Selected as the winning enterprise target path.

The target cloud architecture was designed according to the Google Cloud Architecture Framework, transforming the monolithic JEE middleware into modern containerized microservices orchestrated on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), coupled with an enterprise AlloyDB for PostgreSQL cluster.

In a recent development, the cornerstone of the migration was converting over 1.2 million lines of deeply intertwined Oracle PL/SQL procedural logic into PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL. The team utilized Google Cloud Database Migration Service (DMS) with its built-in Conversion Workspaces and Gemini-assisted AI code refactoring to accelerate bulk transformations.

While DMS automatically converted the majority of standard DDL constructs, functions, and queries, the remaining (~15%) involved complex Oracle proprietary idioms that required targeted engineering remediation. Couple of examples of the manual intervention.

Technical Pattern & Remediation.

Modernized AlloyDB PL/pgSQL Equivalent.

Architectural Remediation & Runtime Impact.

TYPE_L := array_append(TYPE_L, rec); or TYPE_L[cardinality(TYPE_L)+1] := rec;.

Replaced unsupported .EXTEND method on nested tables with native PostgreSQL array concatenation and dynamic index expansion.

SELECT ROWNUM FROM PTY_IM WHERE ROWNUM <= N;.

SELECT s.idx FROM generate_series(1, N) AS s(idx);.

Eliminated physical dummy table hacks (PTY_IM) in favor of in-memory, set-returning generator functions with zero disk I/O.

In April 2026, the modernized DynaPORT platform on Google Cloud went live in production at one of the newest ports in India, achieving a seamless, low downtime cutover. By Aug’26, 3 more terminals have gone live on this.

Modernized Google Cloud & AlloyDB Stack.

Variable query latency during batch spikes; table bloat requiring manual DBA reindexing.

Upto 2x transactional throughput, sub-second read query responses, automated ML vacuuming and memory optimization.

Complex SAN failover; multi-minute outages during planned database maintenance.

Sub-second automatic failover, 99.99% availability SLA inclusive of maintenance, zero transaction loss.

Multi-week release cycles; high-risk manual database patching; frequent regression concerns.

Containerized rolling updates on GKE and non-blocking transactional DDL deployments in AlloyDB.

Punitive per-core enterprise licenses; high on-prem hardware and maintenance overhead.

About 50% reduction in database TCO; completely open-source compatible with transparent, predictable cloud pricing.

Rigid vertical hardware limits; slow hardware procurement cycles.

Instantaneous horizontal elasticity across GKE container pods and AlloyDB read pools.

The successful cloud migration of DynaPORT yields three fundamental architectural lessons for enterprise IT leaders:.

Do Not Throw Away Proven Intellectual Property: Fully rewriting mission-critical procedural logic into application code is often a high-risk anti-pattern. Migrating from Oracle PL/SQL to open PL/pgSQL on an accelerated engine like AlloyDB preserves decades of tested business rules while modernizing the infrastructure platform.

Select Database Engines Built for Cloud Realities: Standard open-source relational engines often struggle with extreme enterprise throughput without extensive tuning. AlloyDB’s disaggregated storage architecture, columnar acceleration, and built-in ML intelligence provide the enterprise muscle needed to replace legacy commercial database engines.

Containerize Application Workloads on GKE: Decoupling the application tier into independently scalable container pods on Google Kubernetes Engine provides the elasticity and resilience necessary to absorb rapid operational surges without affecting core database stability.

Training a coding model to paint watercolours with TRL and OpenEnv

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model.
  • According to recent reports, the video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet.
  • Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model. The model writes JavaScript through p5.brush, a library that "adds natural drawing tools to p5.js". The video went viral fast, over 1.5M views at the time of writing.

According to recent reports, the video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet. His site says a full technical report is coming, so ensure you follow him. The original idea is his, coming from the art and design side, where his skills are way beyond mine. My attempt is on the engineering side, reproducing the recipe in the open with every piece published.

Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.

In this article I try and reproduce his idea with TRL and OpenEnv. The reference pool dataset, the RL environment, the training scripts and the trained models, all open.

The whole pipeline runs on Hugging Face, end to end:.

Once the two Spaces are up, the recipe is one command. Duplicate the environment and the scorer model, set two environment variables for the reward mix, and launch:.

The rest of this article is the story of getting there, and every piece is in the repo.

I have followed the original blog step by step, and only changed something when strictly needed. Every idea of my own went into a list instead of into the experiment, and that list became "What I would try next" at the end, next to the full list of published artifacts. If you have already read his post, the framing and the reward design will be familiar. The upcoming material is the open implementation, the hand-rated pool, and three reward mixes trained and compared, and it starts at The RL environment you need to build.

According to recent reports, the paintings look loose, imperfect, handmade, at a moment when image models produce perfect (statistically average) pictures. My guess is that this contrast is a major part of why the video went viral. It reminded me of the early days of generative AI art, when the point was to explore the medium. DeepDream (2015) was a debugging tool that people turned into art, works like Edmond de Belamy (2018) came from artists probing what a GAN could do, and artists like Mario Klingemann spent those years making dreamy portraits with neural networks.

According to recent reports, this project feels closer to those early days. In his thesis, Surya describes the path that led here. He started by prompting text-to-image models, where the prompt is the only lever you can pull, and more detail buys more control only up to a point. Training the model itself goes further. The other half of the idea is the medium. The model writes a program of about 150 lines of JavaScript that paints the image. That model output is code. You can read it, edit it and run it again, and the decision behind each brushstroke is visible. And the style comes from a restriction where the model is only allowed ten of the library's methods. More on that below.

In that same period, Anna Ridler photographed thousands of tulips, hand-labelled every one, exhibited the dataset itself as the artwork, and later trained a model on it. I found her work through the references AI agents brought back while building this project and loved it because this project does something very similar by curating a set of images by hand, and then training against them.

According to recent reports, most of the recent RL work on language models uses rewards you can verify. For example, math problems with a known answer, code that passes tests, or graders that are right or wrong and cheap to run. This project is closer to the older exception, RLHF, where the model learns a reward model from human preferences.

Here the reward is aesthetic preference. There is no correct answer. The real question of the project is whether you can do RL over taste.

The reward, as his blog defines it and as the RL environment I built implements it:.

HPSv3 is an open 7B preference model. Give it an image and a text description, and it returns a score for how much a person would prefer that image. It was trained on a large set of human choices between pairs of images, so its score is an average of many people's taste. The pairwise judge is Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, a general vision model called through HF Inference Providers. The pairwise judge sees the candidate painting next to four references randomly selected from the pool, guided by a written description of what to weigh (bleeds, translucent washes, soft edges), each comparison in both presentation orders, and its score is the share of comparisons the candidate wins. Its only standard is the pool, so its score is my taste, as encoded in those ratings.

Those are the weights Narreddi converged on. The pool defines taste here. That moves the work from tuning hyperparameters to building the set that decides what is beautiful.

It has been revealed that I trained three runs with this reward. They differ only in how the weight splits between the two model judges:.

According to recent reports, I started with hps-only to validate that the pipeline could learn at all. Once the reward was going up and the metrics were healthy, there was no reason to run it longer, so I launched the two longer runs instead. The question that the longer runs ask is how much of HPSv3's power can you hand to the pairwise judge? The more weight the judge carries, the more the reward means my taste instead of everyone's, and the harder it should be to climb. Incidentally, if you push it far enough or your style is too far from the average, the model could stop entirely.

Fortunately, it did not stop and both runs with the pairwise judge on learned too. The hand-rated pool can steer the policy, at least as far as the metrics and the final paintings show. The numbers are below.

According to recent reports, disclaimer. If we use a frontier model, it can already generate the JavaScript code that paints watercolour from a prompt. That's the starting point. The work here is about teaching a smaller model to do it combined with a person's own artistic preferences.

The environment wraps everything that sits between the model and the reward, including the JavaScript library that the model uses for painting, the system prompt that restricts it, the headless Chromium that renders each sketch, and the gate that rejects cheats.

According to recent reports, the library does more of the work than it seems. p5.brush, by @acamposuribe, simulates a medium rather than drawing shapes: pigment bleeds past the edges of a fill, paper has texture, strokes have mass, flow fields drag brushwork around. When the model calls brush.fillBleed(0.25) it is deciding how far the ink runs.

Note. The author of p5.brush had been trying to teach a machine to paint long before any of this. In 2022 he made a generative art series that hides a diary about teaching p5.js to draw like a child: "It is barely able to use the crayons [...] It cannot follow simple commands. I'm done for today, very infuriating." The series was meant to have three pieces, and he made two. When Surya's video went viral, he quoted it, sharing that diary and saying this work is the third piece arriving on its own.

p5.brush exposes 47 methods. The prompt allows 10: scaleBrushes, noStroke, fill, noFill, fillBleed, fillTexture, beginShape, vertex, endShape and circle. What the other thirty-seven add, lines, hatching, custom brushes, would break the watercolour look. With these ten the model can only paint filled shapes, and the library adds the bleed to every one of them.

Industry observers note that his blog post saved me a lot of time I could have wasted iterating on the prompt. A long API reference makes the model invent methods that do not exist, and his 200 GEPA iterations converged on a strict allowlist with no documentation. I saw the same failures and wrote the allowlist by hand. My only addition to that recipe is one sentence: paint each petal two or three times, a big pass first and a smaller, more opaque one inside it. This small change made my outputs a lot more colorful.

Note. If it's the first time you hear about GEPA, it is an automatic prompt optimizer. A language model reflects in plain words on where the current prompt failed and proposes a better one, and the loop repeats.

The gate is the final piece. The sketch has to compile, use the library instead of direct p5 calls, put real pigment on the canvas, and not try to trick the scorer, for example by writing text on the canvas.

Recent findings suggest that the pool consists of 178 paintings divided into two tiers based on my personal preferences, love and okay. All of them are actually generated by a model. Four open-weight models, called through Inference Providers, wrote p5.brush sketches, each one working from a real, openly licensed photo of a hibiscus from iNaturalist. A vision model gave written feedback on every sketch, over three refinement iterations. Every final render was then rated one at a time, by me, and 178 made the cut.

Industry observers note that here I chose four different families of models to test their different styles. These four were the open models that produced a valid sketch every time in a quick reliability check, and two other candidates were dropped for failing it. If you want to produce your own pool, you might choose others.

Sources indicate that the tiers do real work in the reward. When the pairwise judge draws four references, half come from love and half from okay, so the policy always faces some rivals it can sometimes beat, and a win pays the same against either tier. This is one of my few deliberate changes: the original compares against its top tier only, and I kept the easier tier in the draw so a weak early policy still gets signal.

No human-made painting is in there, which is a real limitation. p5.brush is a niche library, and the human work that exists in it with accessible code is a handful of pieces, nowhere near what a training corpus would need, as his blog also notes.

According to recent reports, the interesting idea here, as I've already discussed previously, is that the model will learn to imitate what the pool contains. If we point the environment at a different dataset, the reward would automatically change without touching a single line of code. For the dataset I generated and openly share, I also include the source sketch.

If we look closer at the judges, the two of them answer different questions. HPSv3 decides whether it is a flower, and the pairwise judge decides whether it is well painted in the style I chose.

Before anything worked, there was a long stretch of flat reward curves. If you've tried to reproduce a research paper/blog without open artifacts, you probably can relate. Every run tested what I thought was a reasonable theory about what was wrong. A run takes a lot of time, so I queued the next one while still going through the last one's results. As always, starting from something easier that works and then building on top of that was the answer. A simple control task, with no browser and no judges, was the first attempt that learned, and the reason was that my learning rate was just too low.

Recent findings suggest that another change that cost me time to find was adjusting the LoRA parameters correctly. The usual target_modules list assumes a dense model, and Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is a mixture of experts that names most of its projections differently, so the adapter was training ten layers out of forty. I solved this by changing it to all-linear, which reaches every linear layer. The routed experts in this architecture are fused tensors that even all-linear leaves frozen, but everything else gets an adapter, and that was enough to learn.

The fix was four changes in TRL's GRPOTrainer:.

These four changes unlocked the first successful run (hps-only), with the reward clearly improving.

With that configuration, all three runs learn. Both judge runs were launched for 200 steps and stopped at 110, with the reward still climbing slowly. A step takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, and the comparison between mixes was already stable, so I stopped both to save compute. Mean group reward over the first and final third of each run:.

In a recent development, the three curves line up with how much weight my taste carries. The more the judge weighs, the lower the start and the noisier the climb. judge-led spent its first thirty steps nearly flat before it moved. It is the same move that solved the debugging. Shrink the problem until something learns, then add the hard parts back one at a time.

It has been revealed that the pairwise judge term itself climbed in the two runs that used it. The model wins more comparisons against the pool as training advances, which is the claim hps-only could not make. No group in any run collapsed to identical rewards, the GRPO failure mode that kills the gradient. For the curious, the per-metric curves (HPSv3, paint coverage, entropy) are in the repository as CSV.

The full launch command, the hardware and the two environment variables that turn this into the other two runs are in the recipe.

In every run, the first thing the model learned was to stop producing bad paintings, the near-blank canvases and shapeless washes that score under 0.3 in total reward. In hps-only, three quarters of the rise in the group mean comes from bad paintings becoming rare. In the judge runs the collapse is even steeper: rollouts under 0.3 fall from 99 to 16 across judge-led's thirds, and from 37 to 4 in hps-led.

This is why the obvious visual, the best painting of each step, shows almost no difference in hps-only. It moves +0.034 across the run while the median moves +0.155. The learning is visible in the middle of the distribution.

Sources indicate that what the pairwise judge changes is the top. In hps-only, paintings got more reliable without getting better. The quality of the good ones added just +0.03 to the group mean, and once HPSv3 saw petals around a centre and a stem, it stopped asking for more pigment. With the judge on, the other half of the story appears. Better here means closer to the pool, so closer to what I rated as "good" or something I liked more. That added +0.12 in judge-led and +0.16 in hps-led, the best of each step rose too, and paint coverage doubled in both runs (0.11 to 0.23, and 0.13 to 0.30) where hps-only barely moved it. With a reference left to beat, a good painting can still get better, and the model starts being rewarded for using more pigment.

One more finding. The model ignores an explicit instruction, and it is right to. The system prompt asks for fifteen to thirty filled shapes. If we look at the real mean, it is between 7 and 9, and n_shapes barely correlates with reward in any run (+0.000, −0.14, +0.07). The policy is not rewarded for obeying that sentence, so it does not obey it.

There is also a ceiling on the hps-only route. If every rollout matched its good ones, that run's mean would sit at 0.771. Whether more steps would break it is an open question.

In a recent development, the paintings also show something that the tables miss. Within each run, they all look similar. As training advances, the rewards inside each group get closer together, and the median paintings in the opening video look like takes of the same flower. That is GRPO doing what it is designed to do with a pool built from one subject. The pool decides what counts as variety, the same way it decides what counts as quality. If the reward only pays for matching one flower, the model learns to paint that one flower. More diverse output would need a more diverse pool, and building one is more curation work. Surya's newer compositions are an example of this. Alex Yango's animal paintings are the same recipe with different choices in the pool. This is the biggest difference between an aesthetic reward and a maths grader. Behind the number there is a very human job, deciding what belongs in the reward set. Jason Liu's essay on taste notes the general version in one line. AI shifted the bottleneck from making to noticing.

Surya closes his blog with some of his favourites. Instead of picking mine, below is a wall with the 178 paintings the reward scored highest across the two judge runs, the same number the reference pool holds, in no particular order. Open it and pick your own.

It has been revealed that to choose, you looked at many and kept a few, and that is exactly the job that built the reward of this project. Every painting of every run, with its sketch and its reward, is in the rollouts datasets, and browsable in this gallery.

It has been revealed that since the reward was partly based on my taste, it is fair to close with my verdict as a viewer. To my eye, judge-led is the run that ends up the most diverse and the most artistically interesting. hps-led paints convincing watercolours, but its best ones share a soft, wet-on-wet look that is almost a style of its own. hps-only converges the hardest, and most of its paintings settle on the same colours. You can judge for yourself in the gallery, which has every painting of every run, sortable by step and by reward.

It has been revealed that this project is mostly infra. A run needs a trainer, two Spaces, an inference router and a websocket to stay healthy for hours straight, and every piece that fails quietly turns into a wrong number somewhere else. Half the work is checking that the number you read matches what actually happened.

In a recent development, failures of the infrastructure were entering the reward as zeros. A render that timed out or a scorer that did not answer scored the same as a bad painting, 0.0 inside the group. Across all my runs that was about 1.5% of rollouts, and in the worst run it reached 5.2%. That trains the model on noise, so those paths now return None and the rollout is excluded from the group.

Sources indicate that I also found a bug in OpenEnv, and sent the fix upstream. The client keeps one persistent websocket, and a socket closed by the far end stayed cached, so every later call failed even though the environment was healthy. It cost me two half-finished runs to find it. The fix is submitted upstream, and the runs debuted with it have been running clean since.

Recent findings suggest that the reward of a step depends on which references it drew. The pairwise judge samples four references per step, so every step faces a different set of rivals, and some draws are simply harder. GRPO itself is mostly safe, because advantages are computed inside the group and a hard draw moves the whole group together. The curve I was reading was not safe, and some of what looked like a bad step was just a hard draw. The image above is one example. Step 12 scored half a point below step 11 mostly because it drew the hardest references of the run, while the paintings themselves look close.

Rounded numbers, and only for the runs that finished.

According to recent reports, A step is eight rollouts and takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, of which 70 to 80% is rendering. A single render takes 69 to 96 seconds against a 90 second deadline. Part of that is expected, the Space has no GPU, so Chromium renders the WEBGL canvas in software and p5.brush's bleeds and textures are heavy pixel work. Even so, I expected it to be faster, and I have not found the full cause.

A scorer can cost more than the training that uses it: HPSv3 has to be up for the whole run, so pause the Space, or set its sleep timer, when the run ends.

Everything runs on HF Jobs, with the environment as a Docker Space and metrics in trackio.

The rule of this project was to reproduce the recipe with every resource open, not to improve it, so a list of untried ideas piled up along the way. These are the ones I would actually try, in order of how much evidence there is.

Multi-step, and letting the model see what it paints. This is the first thing I would try. The original blog trains single turn, so I trained single turn, and in this setup the model paints with its eyes closed. No image ever goes in, and the only feedback it gets is one number. The evidence that a feedback loop works is the pool itself. The reference paintings came from models iterating three rounds under a vision critic, and the later rounds are better. The material that defines the reward was made with a loop the policy never gets.

Smaller models. There is evidence that 35B is more than needed. In my side experiments a 4B already wrote valid sketches that passed the gate. If a 4B can learn this, the cost of the experiment drops by an order of magnitude.

Other ideas on the list are SFT on the pool sources before starting RL, rewarding pigment explicitly, moving the judge's reference mix from easy to hard as the run advances until only love remains, widening the ten-method allowlist for more visual range (my attempts on this crashed more sketches and broke the watercolour look), and checking how consistent the pairwise judge really is by scoring the same image twice.

And the method is not specific to flowers. Alex Yango painted animals with the same mechanism, and Brendan Hogan trained canvas animations against a pool of hand-rated clips. I had also played with something similar before using Simon Willison's pelican benchmark, where code is rendered to an image and scored.

Recent findings suggest that and underneath all of it sits the question this project cannot close. 178 paintings made by models define what this trained model considers beautiful. The pool is the bottleneck, and it is the part of the pipeline with no principled answer.

For anyone reproducing this, there are two deliberate divergences from Narreddi's recipe, both argued earlier in the article:.

It has been revealed that the rest, all-linear for the LoRA, infrastructure failures returning None instead of 0.0, stopping the judge runs at step 110, are decisions I had to make along the way because his blog does not specify them. His implementation is not published, so I cannot tell whether they match his choices or diverge from them.

It has been revealed that the per-rollout numbers in this article can be recomputed from the published datasets. Nothing here depends on any Space staying switched on.

Recent findings suggest that the method and original idea are Surya Narreddi's. The library is Alejandro Campos Uribe's.

  • Amazon EventBridge Scheduler expands its AWS SDK integrations with 589 new API actions across 81 AWS services, and adds templated targets for the enhanced EventBridge Custom event bus.

Amazon EventBridge Scheduler expands its AWS SDK integrations with 589 new API actions across 81 AWS services, and adds templated targets for the enhanced EventBridge Custom event bus. You can now schedule direct invocations of a broader set of AWS services without writing custom integration code.

Industry observers note that eventBridge Scheduler is a serverless scheduler that allows you to create, run, and manage billions of scheduled events and tasks across more than 270 AWS services, without provisioning or managing the underlying infrastructure. With a upcoming templated target, you can schedule event delivery directly to the Custom event bus using its PutEvents or PutRawEvents API. The templated target also makes it easier to add metadata fields to each event. For example, you can send an event to your bus every night at midnight to start a reconciliation workflow, with no function in between to call the API.

Sources indicate that the upcoming API actions are available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon EventBridge Scheduler is available, subject to the availability of each target service in the Region. The templated targets for the Custom event bus are available in all AWS Regions where the enhanced Custom event bus is available. To learn more, see Using templated targets in EventBridge Scheduler and Using universal targets in EventBridge Scheduler in the Amazon EventBridge Scheduler User Guide. CypherMAS: Benchmarking Routing Reliability in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (186 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33242v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) distribute reasoning across specialized agents that must exchange messages and invoke tools reliably. Existing evaluations typically couple communication with open domain tasks, making it difficult to determine whether a failure arises from reasoning, malformed tool use, lost messages, or forgotten requests. Prior benchmarks do not isolate communication execution or measure routing redundancy against a known optimal path. We introduce CypherMAS, a synthetic benchmark that isolates communication and routing in fixed multi-agent graphs. Agents in chain, star, bipartite, or ring graphs route cyphered messages to remote peers holding the matching decoders; since the optimal route is known, redundant LLM calls can be measured and routing failures may be easily tracked. Across eleven open-weight models from 4B to 753B, small models fail at routing and tool use, dense models above 27B degrade with diameter, and successful runs exceed minimum LLM calls. These findings identify communication reliability as a distinct scaling bottleneck for multi-agent systems and provide a controlled diagnostic for complex multi-agent systems. The source code is freely available: https://github.com/Andoree/CypherMAS.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the course of this year, AI systems have become increasingly capable, potentially increasing their ability to contribute to AI research and development themselves.
  • This report builds on our September blog post on research acceleration at OpenAI⁠, adding new quantitative and qualitative measures of (1) AI uplift across research domains and (2) how humans remain involved in the research process.
  • We are sharing this work because, as we wrote in our frontier policy blueprint⁠⁠ and reiterated in our first research acceleration report⁠, we believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the course of this year, AI systems have become increasingly capable, potentially increasing their ability to contribute to AI research and development themselves. Today, we’re providing an upgrade on the state of research acceleration at OpenAI, based on internal measurements of how coding agents have accelerated and changed the AI development cycle.

This report builds on our September blog post on research acceleration at OpenAI⁠, adding new quantitative and qualitative measures of (1) AI uplift across research domains and (2) how humans remain involved in the research process. Overall, we believe this enhancement provides a broader, though still partial, picture of how research at OpenAI is changing.

We are sharing this work because, as we wrote in our frontier policy blueprint⁠⁠ and reiterated in our first research acceleration report⁠, we believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems.

Industry observers note that as capabilities improve and dramatic AI-driven research acceleration becomes increasingly possible, we will need to solve novel technical and governance complications to maintain human oversight and safely scale AI systems⁠. Transparency about indicators of RSI is therefore essential to inform a public discussion of the capabilities, risks, and required safeguards for increasingly powerful AI; however, our reporting should not be read as an intention to pursue full RSI. We have been heartened to see that several other organizations have recently contributed to the growing body of work measuring AI R&D acceleration1. Our hope is that this expanded report will help sustain and advance these shared measurement norms across the industry.

We structure this report in three sections, each focused on a different aspect of AI research:.

We believe organizing the results in this way provides a useful framework for reasoning about how AI is used in research and how that use might contribute to improvements in model capabilities.

Industry observers note that AI research uses several inputs, including data, AI tools (e.g., coding agents), human labor, and compute. In this report, we focus on AI tools as an input to research. Specifically, we document how the intensity of coding-agent use varies across teams and changes over time. Further, while we do not directly report changes in labor costs, we examine how the share of spending on research labor has changed relative to spending on other factors over time.

It has been revealed that since our first report⁠, agentic AI usage within the research organization has continued to increase exponentially. At API list prices, the median researcher now uses around $2,400 USD per day on agentic AI tools, and the 90th percentile researcher now around $23,000 USD per day, up 62% and 105% respectively from $1,500 and $11,000 in September.2 This trend in increased agentic usage captures a wide variety of changes including increased activity, shifts to more expensive models, and changes to model behavior and agentic harnesses.

We next turn to the average number of “agent workdays” per researcher per day, where we define every eight hours of agent use as one agent workday. In contrast to agentic spend, agent workdays better capture the amount of “wall clock time” agents spend working, but do not account for changes in model capabilities or pricing.

Overall, agent workdays per researcher have risen from 0.5 agent workdays per researcher to 5.7 agent workdays per researcher, an elevenfold increase, with the largest increase in teams focused on pretraining and posttraining. On those teams, agent runtime averaged roughly eight workdays per researcher per calendar day. In scaling and infrastructure, the average was roughly four. We note that this workday metric generally includes interactive use only, so it may undercount automations.

Recent findings suggest that our September analysis⁠ highlighted increasing use of concurrent agents by researchers, including subagents and multiple sessions. We extend this analysis further in time and provide more granular bucketing. By mid-October, more than two-thirds of included researchers averaged a daily peak of at least four agents working concurrently and more than 10% averaged at least sixteen concurrent agents.

We next compare monthly API-equivalent spending on agentic AI use with monthly non-equity compensation for human researchers. We track this ratio to see how the allocation between agent and human labor changes as models become more capable. Although the ratio we report excludes equity, which generally accounts for 70 to 80% of target compensation for researchers at OpenAI, we believe it still provides a partial yet informative view of this spending allocation.

As of September 2026, the API-equivalent value of agentic AI use in OpenAI’s research organization was about twice its non-equity compensation, with higher ratios in pretraining and posttraining than in other parts of the research organization. Despite this, internal deployment, which combines internal Codex, ChatGPT, and API usage, accounts for only 2% of total research compute.

It has been revealed that labor costs include salary, overtime, bonuses, benefits, and employer taxes. Equity, which generally accounts for 70 to 80% of target compensation for researchers, is excluded.

According to recent reports, finally, we examine how researchers allocate their time across research areas. We first collected individual-level contributions from researchers in the form of organization-public Slack posts, pull requests, and internal documents from January through September 2026. We then used classifiers to group these contributions into research areas, and each researcher-week was divided equally across that researcher’s verified projects for the week. This provides a proxy for where researchers were directing their attention.

Importantly, unlike our other analyses, the “research area” we classify here does not correspond to formal reporting lines. For example, a researcher on a posttraining team who spends half their time on infrastructure improvements would be estimated as contributing half a workweek to Scaling / Infrastructure Contributions and half to Posttraining Contributions. This allows us to create a robust measurement of where researchers are actively spending time even if they do not formally shift teams.

We find that the amount of researcher time dedicated to each of the areas we identify has grown over the course of 2026. Notably, using this methodology, we find that Safety & Alignment saw the largest absolute increase across any research area, almost doubling in documented workweek contributions since the start of the year due to a combination of new hires and existing researchers shifting their focus toward safety projects. This research area covers workstreams such as alignment evals, monitorability, and reward hacking research. A notable inflection point that we measure in the growth of Safety & Alignment coincides with the aftermath of the Hugging Face incident⁠ in July, and OpenAI’s subsequent work to develop and improve safety cases for frontier AI training⁠.

In a recent development, we note that the distinction between research areas, and especially posttraining versus safety and alignment, is nontrivial and we may iterate on the definition over time. The methods section below describes examples of high-level workstreams.

Sources indicate that to better understand how agent use might affect research productivity, we next examine how the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI is changing. The productivity gains from new technologies depend in part on how work is reorganized around them. As agents improve, researchers may change which tasks they delegate to AI, how they oversee and coordinate agents’ work, and which projects they pursue. Below, we report both quantitative and qualitative measures of how AI is changing the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI. Together, these different types of data contribute to a (partial) view of how researchers are reorganizing their work around agents and how researchers remain in the loop today.

Our September analysis⁠ highlighted that agents became more likely to complete tasks successfully without human intervention, including tasks estimated to require several hours of human work. Using an updated methodology (see the methods section below), we find that this trend has generally continued. Importantly, as agents have become more capable, researchers may also have changed the types of tasks delegated within each duration bucket. As a result, changes in zero-intervention success rates within these buckets may reflect both capability improvements and researchers’ changing choices about when and how to use agents.

In a recent development, alongside these trends by estimated duration, we also examine how success varies across the different types of tasks researchers might choose to delegate. We report estimated success rates by category and task, using the O*NET AI R&D taxonomy⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) developed by Epoch AI. Unsurprisingly, our results suggest that models are not equally good across all task categories: for instance, from August 1, 2026 through October 18, 2026, estimated success rates without human intervention was higher for Communicate (69%) and Analyze (58%) than for Build (43%). Similarly at the task level, estimated success rates were higher for tasks such as monitoring runs for issues (79%) and answering technical questions (72%), whereas they were lower for writing code for inference and serving stacks (25%) and building evaluation, reinforcement-learning, and agent environments (29%). So long as model performance on AI R&D-related tasks is heterogeneous, lower-performing categories and tasks could become bottlenecks to high overall uplift.

Recent findings suggest that our September analysis⁠ reported how research employee AI use was split across output tokens using the same O*NET AI R&D taxonomy⁠(opens in a newly introduced window). Below, we report how often researchers used coding agents for individual tasks. This puts relatively higher weight on short tasks such as answering technical questions compared to token-intensive tasks such as launching and monitoring a training run or implementing a complex feature.

Sources indicate that we next turn to researchers’ own assessments of how AI is changing their work. Through surveys and interviews, we examine how researchers value coding agents, how they come up with research ideas, and how they have adapted their workflows.

Recent findings suggest that from late August to early September 2026, we conducted a survey of 101 research staff to understand AI uplift, centered around the following hypothetical: “Suppose your team’s access to all coding agents better than GPT-5.2 was revoked for the next 3 months. How much would you trade to restore frontier coding agents?” The median researcher reported being willing to trade:.

In a recent development, researchers also reported that their team would need a median of three months to complete work of equal value to their last month of work if they were not allowed to use coding agents (i.e., if they were only allowed to use GitHub Copilot + ChatGPT). While it is important to note potential concerns with the accuracy of self-reports, as well as the ad-hoc nature of our survey sampling strategy, these results are consistent with researchers attributing significant value to AI uplift in their work.

Bars show the weighted share of answers in each range. Dashed lines mark the weighted medians.

According to recent reports, in a separate survey in late October, we also asked whether respondents expected to be more productive in their daily work with our latest internal model or with help from both a mid-career human research engineer and a 2024 model such as o1-preview. 27 of the 28 respondents chose or leaned toward the latest internal model. The remaining respondent did not choose between the two options as posed and stated they would pick GPT-6 Astra over the human-assisted option.

We are also interested in tracking progress in AI-driven idea generation, since the ability to develop and vet conceptual research ideas (research taste) may be a bottleneck for recursive self-improvement. To measure this, we asked one to four researchers who made key contributions in each of three areas (pretraining, posttraining, and safety monitoring) to name one to three ideas they considered most important to the GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra releases. We then asked how those ideas originated and what role, if any, AI played in developing them.

For both releases, posttraining and safety monitoring researchers said that, to their knowledge, people came up with all the ideas they named, and models helped implement them. Pretraining researchers likewise attributed the ideas they identified for GPT-6 Astra entirely to people.

It has been revealed that for GPT-6.2 Astra, pretraining researchers described developing ideas in conversation with Codex. One credited Codex with identifying key insights as they worked through an idea together. Another remarked the main idea was theirs, but it only started working well after Codex suggested a change.

Lastly, to capture qualitative evidence on workflow changes, we also interviewed ten researchers from pretraining, posttraining, and safety on how they used agents. Across these interviews, five main themes emerged, which we summarize below:.

Sources indicate that beyond changes in research inputs and workflows, we also want to understand whether AI use is accelerating research progress. To inform this question, we present three measures. Two of them—lines of code and the number of research experiments—were included in our September analysis⁠. These measures are straightforward to track, but increases in these measures of research activity do not necessarily imply faster research progress. We therefore also introduce OpenAI ECI, an OpenAI-specific internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index, which is one methodology to track changes in model capabilities as a more direct measure of research outcomes.

It has been revealed that we first report how many lines of code are changed per active contributor over time. This measure has continued to increase sharply during 2026 relative to the pre-2025 average. Note that we have made several methodological updates since our September analysis⁠. We now show a 28-day trailing average instead of quarterly averages, providing a more detailed view of changes over time. We have also revised the criteria for which code changes we include (in particular excluding tests), as described in Methods .

Industry observers note that as in our September report⁠, we also track the number of experiments run per active experimenter over time. Over the four weeks ending October 18, logged experiments per active experimenter averaged 1.68 times the 2025 baseline.

Lastly, we report progress on a metric meant to capture advancements in the capabilities of our models. The Epoch Capabilities Index⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) is widely used to measure the progress trend in general AI capabilities. The methodology behind OpenAI ECI (OECI) is very similar to Epoch’s methodology, but OECI uses a combination of public benchmarks and OpenAI internal benchmarks. Here, we graph the OECI of 20 publicly released OpenAI models and 28 other models.

Industry observers note that we find that the OECI frontier for OpenAI models has increased by 16.4 points per year since August 2025, compared to a trend that Epoch observed of 14 points per year⁠(opens in a fresh window) since late 2024. Note that OpenAI models score higher relative to competitors on OECI than they do on Epoch’s ECI, likely due to differences in the benchmark mixture.

We plan to continue monitoring OpenAI ECI and other top-level capability metrics to determine whether capabilities progress is accelerating due to RSI.

Vertical lines are 90% bootstrap intervals. The trendline is fit on the 9 record-setting OpenAI releases.

Overall, our findings extend the picture from our September report⁠: researchers are using agents more intensively, delegating more work, and adapting their workflows around models’ capabilities and limitations. However, this uplift isn’t uniform across all research workflows, and agents today still have significant flaws.

We note that the historical trends and metrics we report (which involve significant human-AI collaboration) may not be predictive of future AI-driven progress. For instance, we recently saw sudden and rapid breakthroughs in mathematics⁠ produced by frontier models. As our models become increasingly autonomous and capable for research, we are monitoring for similarly rapid breakthroughs in deep learning.

Sources indicate that importantly, as AI becomes better at improving itself, competitive pressures and governance challenges will increase, and a key task⁠ will be to ensure humanity remains a part of the process. We hope releasing this data will inform discussions on pacing model capabilities and the governance of recursive self-improvement.

Going forward, we will continue to refine the methods underlying the metrics reported here. We also hope to expand our reporting to provide additional information in a number of areas, including, but not limited to:.

Sources indicate that while the science of empirically measuring AI R&D acceleration is relatively young, it is rapidly growing across the research frontier. So far, Anthropic has independently released three⁠(opens in a new window) separate⁠(opens in a new window) reports⁠(opens in a new window) documenting how internal model deployments have accelerated the AI research process. Section 3.4.2 of the Gemini 4 Argon Safety and Security Report⁠(opens in a new window) outlines empirically the growing share of AI-written code internally at Google DeepMind. In collaboration with Anthropic, METR released an acceleration report⁠(opens in a new window) estimating the amount that internal Claude models have accelerated the capabilities frontier.

We note that OpenAI researchers do not presently have agentic coding quotas.

Sources indicate that on August 21st, OpenAI internally deployed a temporary harness efficiency improvement. We found that this internal deployment coincided with a sharp decrease in input token utilization, which appears to have severely depressed the documented amount of internal token spend. This harness change was gradually reverted across internal deployments for reasons unrelated to spend starting on September 10th, and we find that token spend rapidly increases afterwards.

arXiv:2611.33238v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose two general, distribution-free test statistics for binary Sequential Hypothesis Testing (SHT) and Sequential Change Point Detection (SCPD) respectively, in streaming environments where the data (e.g., network traffic metadata) are too complicated for the exact probabilistic modeling required by conventional likelihood ratio-driven tests. Our framework also addresses the challenge of information asymmetry, where data is available only from the null/pre-change regime and not from the alternative/post-change one such as zero-day attacks or emerging disease related regimes. The proposed statistics monitor the errors of a predictive or reconstructive machine learning model trained solely on null/pre-change data, relying on imperfect generalization (the model's performance will degrade when deployed on data from the alternative/post-change class). Under mild assumptions on the model's errors, we establish rigorous analytical guarantees: strict non-asymptotic error control for SHT, and explicit bounds on the Average Run Length (ARL) and the Expected Detection Delay (EDD) for SCPD. Extensive evaluations in target tracking, chaotic dynamical systems, and real-world network security datasets, demonstrate that our framework consistently satisfies prescribed constraints where existing algorithms succumb to inflated missed detections and/or false alarms. Finally, because our methods operate on scalar errors without requiring online retraining or kernel evaluations, they are highly scalable.

According to recent reports, today, AWS Billing and Cost Management unveils new APIs that let you view your AWS payment information through the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI. With these APIs, you can check your account balance, find invoices that are due or past due, see which payments and credit memos were applied to each invoice, and confirm that the payment methods on your account are active. You can call the APIs from your own tools or through an AI agent.

Previously, finance teams had to sign in to the console to find past-due invoices, match payments to invoices, or check whether a payment method was still active. Now you can automate these checks with APIs such as GetFinancialRecord, BatchGetFinancialRecord, ListFinancialRecords, GetAccountBalance, GetPaymentInstrument and ListPaymentInstruments. You can integrate the APIs with your accounts payable systems to monitor past-due balances and reconcile AWS invoices on your own schedule.

In a recent development, the APIs are available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region, and available to customers in all commercial AWS Regions.

To learn more, visit the AWS Payments API Reference.
